topics.name: Workflow
topics.vision: Break complex work into subtasks, manage the dependencies between them, and assemble the results.
topics.question: One person with agentic AI now matches a hackathon team of five. Do we still need to decompose work across people?

topics.name: Task assignment
topics.vision: Match workers to tasks that fit their skills and interests, so requesters get speed and workers stay steadily employed.
topics.question: When agents take most tasks, what is left to assign to people, and who decides?

topics.name: Hierarchy
topics.vision: Crowd teams with managers and reviewers, so groups can take on large, complex work.
topics.question: Who manages whom when a team includes agents?

topics.name: Real-time response
topics.vision: Crowds on call that respond within seconds for work that cannot wait.
topics.question: Models answer instantly. When do we still need people on call?

topics.name: Synchronous collaboration
topics.vision: Strangers build rapport fast enough to work together on a task within an hour.
topics.question: If one person with AI can do a team's work, why do we still work together?

topics.name: Quality control
topics.vision: Keep work quality high, including for open-ended and expert tasks where no gold standard exists.
topics.question: Who catches the AI's failures, and how do teams agree on how far to trust its output?

topics.name: Crowds guiding AIs
topics.vision: People do the work AI systems cannot yet do. The paper warned that workers “may end up training machines to replace them.”
topics.question: Did they? And who holds the harness now when AI fails, bug-bounty style?

topics.name: AIs guiding crowds
topics.vision: Software steers crowd work, catching errors before they spread through the crowd.
topics.question: AI now leads much of the work. Where do people still steer?

topics.name: Platforms
topics.vision: New platforms that reshape the relationship between workers and requesters.
topics.question: MTurk shuts down on September 30, 2026. What replaces it, and what do workers get?

topics.name: Job design
topics.vision: Work that builds skills and meaning, well beyond dull piecework dressed up as a game.
topics.question: What work next to AI would we be proud to see our children do?

topics.name: Reputation and credentials
topics.vision: Lasting, portable reputation, like references and work histories in traditional firms.
topics.question: How do you build a track record when an AI did half the work?

topics.name: Motivation and rewards
topics.vision: Rewards matched to workers’ diverse motives and ambitions, beyond small payments per task.
topics.question: What should overseeing AI pay, and what happens when tokens cost what they really cost?

topics.name: Governance and the social contract
topics.vision: Missing from the 2013 framework. Proposed at CrowdCamp 2026: a social contract between people, technology and the environment, with collective action as a counterweight to AI.
topics.question: Who writes that contract? Can crowds organize the way labor unions once did?

blocks.name: Mechanisms and Roles in Human–AI Interaction

contents.title: Interactive Human-AI Alignment: Interaction Mechanisms as Building Blocks for Alignment Design
contents.abstract: Recent AI alignment work often frames alignment as a pre-deployment optimization problem: collect human feedback, learn preferences or principles, fine-tune the model, and deploy an aligned system. This framing has produced major progress, but it under-specifies what happens once AI systems are used in situated, long-term, and social contexts. This position paper emphasizes human-AI alignment as an ongoing interaction problem. We synthesize five alignment questions: how people express intent, how AI decides when to act or ask, how people evaluate success, how AI adapts over repeated use, and how humans adapt their trust, expectations, and behavior.

contents.title: When AI Says "I have been in similar situations": Synthetic Lived Experience in Peer-like Caregiver Support
contents.abstract: Caregivers often turn to online communities for informational and emotional support. In these spaces, peers frequently draw on personal narratives to respond to emotionally complex caregiving situations. As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly designed as peer-like sources of support, they introduce a critical tension: AI can provide immediate, private, and nonjudgmental support, but it cannot authentically possess the lived experiences that make human peer support meaningful. Yet, when prompted to sound peer-like, LLMs may generate language that implies lived experience, such as ``I’ve been in similar situations.'' This creates a synthetic lived experience paradox: the same experiential language that may make AI support feel warm, relatable, and peer-like can also falsely position the system as someone with lived experience. We examine this paradox in the context of family caregivers of people living with Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (AD/ADRD). Drawing on caregiver support exchanges from online communities and peer-prompted responses from three LLMs---LLaMA, GPT-4o-mini, and MedGemma---we analyze how human peers use personal narratives and how AI incorporates similar narrative forms. Our psycholinguistic analysis shows that online peer responses used significantly more first-person and past-focused language than prompted peer-like AI responses. Qualitatively, we identify seven types of personal narratives in human peer support and show that AI often captures their emotional work, but can generalize, flatten, or fabricate their experiential grounding. These findings reveal a narrative authenticity gap: peer-like AI can generate synthetic lived experience without the real experience that makes peer support meaningful. We argue that caregiver-support AI systems need mechanisms to distinguish supportive peer-like framing from fabricated lived experience, ensuring that models can offer warmth and validation without falsely positioning themselves as experiential peers.

contents.title: Exploring the Design Space of AI Simulation-Based Communication Training: A Qualitative Study of Online Peer Counselor Preferences
contents.abstract: A growing body of work uses AI-based simulation to teach communication skills, but current simulation-based communication training (SBCT) systems make inconsistent choices on design dimensions that prior theory identifies as critical: how skills are modeled, when feedback is given, and how self-reflection is scaffolded. These choices are especially consequential in domains like peer counseling, where trainees navigate emotional ambiguity and must anticipate how their words will land. Through prototype-driven and semi-structured interviews with 16 online peer counselors, we explore this design space of SBCT systems by eliciting reactions to 10 prototypes varying across the three dimensions. We find that participants wanted support throughout the process of composing responses (interpreting support-seekers' messages, formulating goals, and anticipating consequences), not solely evaluation of finished messages. Participants also saw feedback timing as instilling mindsets about real-world consequences in sensitive communication, such as signaling proactive prevention of harm through feedback before sending messages. Participants described and anticipated different needs for novice and experienced trainees, suggesting a progression of training environments that adjusts simulation realism and scaffolding to experience level. We conclude with design implications for AI SBCT and peer counseling training, including a tension between users' desire for validation and the need for ambiguity tolerance and authentic communication.

contents.title: When the Interviewer Is a Bot: Behavior, Breakdowns, and Trust in MLLM-Led Interviews
contents.abstract: Semi-structured interviews are a cornerstone of qualitative research but remain labor-intensive. We present InterviewBot, an MLLM-powered system designed to automate semi-structured interviewing through a hybrid conversational architecture that balances rigid protocol adherence with adaptive, context-aware probing. We report on a practice study (N=15) comprising bot-led interviews via a screen-sharing interface, followed by human-led reflection sessions. Framing automated interviewing as a human-computation data-collection task, we contribute (i) a turn-level behavioral coding of an MLLM interviewer (N_turns=428), (ii) a within-subject comparison of the bot against a human interviewer of the same participants, and (iii) a taxonomy of collection breakdowns, alongside the qualitative dynamics of disclosure, legitimacy, and grounding. Our analysis of these reflections reveals three key dynamics: (1) Disclosure Calibration, where participants felt reduced social pressure but sometimes offered shallower responses; (2) Contextual Legitimacy, where trust depended on perceived stakes and institutional signaling rather than just capability; and (3) Conversational Grounding, where participants relied on content-grounded paraphrasing over generic social fillers to assess active listening. We conclude with design implications for depth control, transparent handoffs, and non-templated listening mechanisms to support human-centered interview automation.

contents.title: Towards Actionable Surgical Team Dynamics: from Teamwork to Counterfactual Annotations
contents.abstract: Modeling team interactions in high-stakes environments such as surgical operating rooms is critical for understanding how coordination, communication, and individual behaviors jointly shape team performance and safety outcomes. However, existing multimodal datasets in this domain are often fragmented across modalities, annotation schemes, and formats, limiting their ability to support integrated analyses of real-world collaborative processes. We address this limitation by introducing a curated and extended multimodal dataset for surgical team interaction analysis, built from real operating room recordings. Starting from an existing corpus, we construct a harmonized and analysis-ready version of the data by providing temporally consistent speaker diarization, bilingual (German and English) transcripts, and aligned multi-level annotations capturing team performance, interaction processes, and individual characteristics. Leveraging expert human annotations, team performance is assessed using a standardized surgical teamwork evaluation protocol, while interaction quality and individual attributes are annotated through structured rating schemes covering collaboration, group dynamics, and non-technical skills. To further support the study of coordination breakdowns and performance variability, we introduce counterfactual annotations that describe plausible alternative team outcomes in the presence of observed interaction failures, enabling analysis of how specific behavioral patterns may relate to different trajectories of team performance. In addition, we provide structured temporal and relational representations designed to support computational modeling of teamwork processes and the design of AI-assisted collaborative systems. Overall, the dataset is designed to support the study of how individual actions, interaction patterns, and team-level processes jointly contribute to team outcomes in surgical settings. It provides a unified resource for analyzing collaborative behavior in complex, real-world environments and enables both predictive modeling and behavioral analysis of team coordination in high-stakes domains.

contents.title: Schemex: Discovering Structural Abstractions from Examples
contents.abstract: Creative and communicative work is often underpinned by implicit structures, such as the Hero's Journey in storytelling, design patterns in software, or chord progressions in music. People often learn these structures from examples - a process known as schema induction. However, because schemas are abstract and implicit, they are difficult to discover: shared structural patterns are obscured by surface-level variation, and balancing generality with specificity is challenging. We present Schemex, an interactive AI workflow that systematically supports schema induction by decomposing it into three stages: clustering examples, abstracting candidate schemas, and contrastively refining them by generating new instances and comparing against originals. Studies show that Schemex produces more actionable schemas than a frontier baseline without sacrificing generalizability, with participants uncovering deep and nuanced structural patterns. We also discuss design implications for the cognitive role of interactive process in structure discovery.

contents.title: Connections between Interactions
contents.abstract: The sciences of interaction have, interestingly, not interacted very much with one another. Organizational behavior and social psychology scholars have investigated human-human interaction for well over a century, producing a rich body of theory on topics ranging from interpersonal trust and negotiation strategy to team cognition and group decision-making. Over the past decades, researchers in human-computer interaction (HCI) and the behavioral sciences have also started studying human-AI interaction, producing a rapidly growing literature on how people collaborate with AI systems across a range of tasks and settings. And in just the last year, people across computer science departments and AI labs have begun studying AI-AI interaction, driven by the rapid deployment of AI agents that interact with one another rather than with humans. These three literatures ask structurally similar questions: How do the characteristics of the actors (i.e., their capabilities, personalities, and complementarities) shape outcomes? How do task characteristics (i.e., the type, incentives, and complexity) moderate the effectiveness of collaboration? How do the processes by which actors coordinate (i.e., the sequencing, communication, and feedback) determine whether the whole exceeds the sum of its parts? Despite this shared conceptual architecture, the three research communities have developed largely in parallel. This paper argues that progress in understanding any one of these interaction types accelerates—and is accelerated by—progress in the other ones. The paper develops this claim by articulating the connections that link all three interaction types, proposing a framework that formalizes these connections, and presenting a research program that leverages them to generate more robust and generalizable knowledge about human-human, human-AI, and AI-AI interaction.

contents.title: Personal Research Ontologies for Personal Open Science
contents.abstract: As researchers conduct their work, they incrementally construct a personal research ontology: a rich, personal understanding of their field and its phenomena. Yet most of this knowledge remains internalized, with only fragments surfacing in publications. This position paper argues that research is fundamentally an act of personal ontology construction and proposes Personal Open Science (POS), a lightweight method for externalizing a researcher’s personal research ontology for downstream use. The method centers on the researcher rather than the publication as the traditional focal unit of Open Science. Building on daily reading habits and a minimal annotation scheme, the approach requires little overhead while producing a structured, explorable representation of a researcher’s interests, influences, and expertise. The annotation requires no machine learning or language models. I demonstrate the method through my own practice of annotating over 45,000 documents across a decade of research. I discuss how externalized personal research ontologies could serve multiple downstream purposes, such as discovery of collaborators and self-reflection by revealing the gap between a researcher’s understanding and the shared ontology of their field. When many researchers externalize their ontologies, the resulting network of overlapping and complementary knowledge structures becomes a resource for collective intelligence, making visible the distributed expertise of a research community and enabling new forms of intellectual coordination across disciplinary boundaries.

contents.title: AI as a Caring Neighbor: Shaping Collective Environmental Health Intelligence through Community Knowledge Ecosystems
contents.abstract: A common focus in collective intelligence pedagogy has been the development of novel technological infrastructures to enable new forms of coordination and problem-solving. Yet in environmental health-disadvantaged communities that face disproportionate exposure risks, collective intelligence already operates through existing civic organizations, whose leaders, volunteers, and citizens interpret science through trusted relationships. Human intermediaries carry out “invisible work” as part of community knowledge infrastructures: interpretive efforts that make communities function but that have not been well attended to in design practices. We investigate what happens when AI is used in such environments, creating new possibilities for community-level collective intelligence. Based on an eight-month participatory action-research project with a community organization in Newark, New Jersey, we examine how large language models could help redistribute the cognitive burden of communicating about water quality by creating and customizing outreach materials. Rather than inventing collective intelligence from the ground up, we augment the community’s cognitive capacities by distributing knowledge-retrieval and synthesis tasks to AI, while allowing community leaders to retain interpretive control and volunteers to continue carrying relational responsibilities. Through focus groups and interviews with community leaders, volunteers, environmental historians, and affected community members, we identify four key tensions that emerge when AI-augmented collective intelligence is used alongside human collective intelligence. In particular, we examine cognitive delegation vs. oversight workload, relational trust vs. communication scalability, empathy vs. authenticity, and uncertainty-aware messaging vs. engagement. Our findings show that collective intelligence technologies need to engage with the existing community knowledge ecosystems rather than remain alongside them. To augment community interpretive capacities without undermining relational trust and community leadership requires recognizing human mediators as indispensable parts of interpretive processes in which their contributions create actionable knowledge.

contents.title: Agents Are Instruments, Not Pilots: Capturing Expert Signal as Reliability Infrastructure for Agentic AI
contents.abstract: Agentic AI systems are entering regulated expert workflows in audit, legal, clinical, and financial domains. When these systems fail, the information needed to repair them often comes from the experts who catch the failure: a reviewer who changes the evidence basis, a manager who reclassifies severity, a team that works around a system limitation. These expert responses are reliability signals, and currently, they evaporate. The collective intelligence of regulated expert organizations depends on the propagation of judgment signals across roles, artifacts, and organizational tiers; agentic AI changes these flows in ways the surrounding instrumentation has not been designed to capture. We propose a five-tier observation framework that identifies where reliability signals arise in agentic systems, from output and execution through coordination, communication, and fitness for purpose, and locates the instrumentation gap at the tiers where expert signal is concentrated and current observability is weakest. From this framework we derive a taxonomy of expert signal for repair: a signal matrix crossing thirteen structural failure modes with seven expert response types, heat-mapped by detection feasibility, and a fractal matrix showing how the same failure modes manifest differently across organizational tiers, heat-mapped by signal evaporation risk. Both gradients are driven by the same variable: proximity to the point where expert judgment and system output meet. Because the correction is the work and not an annotation on it, expert signal cannot be elicited through the labeling, crowdsourcing, or preference-collection methods that assume the human's contribution can be separated from the task and gathered independently. Reliability infrastructure must therefore be designed not only to evaluate outputs, but to preserve the expert judgment that enables organizational learning. The taxonomy is field-grounded, derived from deployed agentic systems in regulated audit monitoring contexts. This paper specifies the instrumentation required to capture judgment without separating it from the work itself.

contents.title: Where can AI be used? Insights from a deep ontology of work activities
contents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to profoundly reshape how work is organized, but we do not yet have deep frameworks for understanding how AI can be used to create collectively intelligent human-AI systems. Here, we provide a comprehensive ontology of work activities that can help systematically analyze and predict where AI can be used. After classifying data from 13,275 AI software applications and 20.8 million robotic systems into the work activities in this ontology, we find a highly uneven distribution of AI market value across activities. The top 1.6% of activities account for over 60% of AI market value. Most of this market value is used in information-based activities (72%), especially creating information (36%), and only 12% is used in physical activities. Interactive activities include both information-based and physical activities and account for 48% of AI market value, much of which (26%) involves transferring information. We also discuss how this systematic framework can help predict at a detailed level where today’s AI systems can and cannot be used and how future AI capabilities may change this.

blocks.name: Delegating to and Coordinating with Agents

contents.title: Partner-Adaptive Delegation in Ad Hoc Teamwork
contents.abstract: When agents collaborate with unfamiliar teammates, they must decide not only how to act, but also when to rely on others. This is challenging because a teammate may be strong on some subtasks but less effective on others, making delegation both useful and risky. Delegating control can improve performance when the teammate has the right skill, but it can also waste time or reduce performance when the teammate is less competent. Delegation also provides useful evidence about the teammate’s competence through their success or failure on the current subtask. We study this tradeoff in ad hoc teamwork, where an agent must learn when to act on its own and when to delegate to an unseen teammate whose strengths vary across subtasks. We propose CoDeT, a competence-belief delegation method that uses factored Bayesian beliefs to estimate teammate competence across subtasks and decide when to delegate. We evaluate CoDeT using a strict complementarity metric, which measures whether teamwork creates value beyond what either agent could achieve alone. Across sequential decision making tasks including Level-Based Foraging and Overcooked-AI, CoDeT achieves positive teamwork value, avoids harmful delegation, and outperforms baselines that do not learn when to delegate. In settings where teammate contributions are consistently useful, CoDeT also recovers delegation strategies that are competitive with strong static engagement policies. These results highlight the benefits of competence-aware delegation for collaboration with unfamiliar teammates whose strengths vary across subtasks.

contents.title: Behavioral Drivers of the Jagged Frontier in Human-AI Collaboration
contents.abstract: AI tools improve knowledge work, but the same tool can help on one task while hurting another. This variation, termed the jagged frontier, is typically attributed to differences in AI capability, but it is unclear whether there are also behavioral factors. Here we show, in a preregistered experiment where 2,234 participants created display ads with a human partner or an AI agent, that the jagged frontier traces to collaboration behavior. Human-AI teams produced higher-quality text but lower-quality images, as independently rated and confirmed in a field experiment on *X*. This asymmetry is predicted by two behavior factors. First, participants delegated writing more ad copy to AI but less image prompts, even though delegation predicted similar quality gains for both. Second, image quality tracked how many candidates teams generated and iterated on. After accounting for both behaviors, the residual image gap is statistically indistinguishable from zero. The jagged frontier in this setting is a property of the collaboration, not of the AI.

contents.title: DoubleAgents: Interactive Simulations for Alignment in Agentic AI
contents.abstract: Agentic workflows promise efficiency, but adoption hinges on whether people can align systems that act on their behalf with their goals, values, and situational expectations. We present DoubleAgents, an agentic planning tool that embeds transparency and control through user intervention, value-reflecting policies, rich state visualizations, and uncertainty flagging for human coordination tasks. A built-in respondent simulation generates realistic scenarios, allowing users to rehearse, refine policies, and calibrate their use of agentic behavior before live deployment. We evaluate DoubleAgents in a two-day lab study (n=10), three deployment studies, and a technical evaluation. Results show that participants initially hesitated to delegate but used simulation to probe system behavior and adjust policies, gradually increasing delegation as agent actions became better aligned with their intentions and context. Deployment results demonstrate DoubleAgents’ real-world relevance and usefulness, showing that simulation helps users effectively manage real-world tasks with higher complexity and uncertainty. We contribute interactive simulation as a practical pathway for users to iteratively align and calibrate agentic systems.

contents.title: AgentDynEx: Nudging the Mechanics and Dynamics of Multi-Agent Simulations
contents.abstract: Multi-agent large language model simulations have the potential to model complex human behaviors and interactions. If the mechanics are set up properly, unanticipated and valuable social dynamics can surface. However, it is challenging to consistently enforce simulation mechanics while still allowing for rich and emergent dynamics. We present AgentDynEx, an AI system that helps set up, track, and repair simulations. Specifically, AgentDynEx introduces milestones that act as checkpoints and failure conditions that act as guardrails to ensure dynamics are relevant and mechanics are respected as the simulation progresses. It also introduces a method called nudging, where the system dynamically reflects on simulation progress and gently intervenes if it begins to deviate from intended outcomes. A technical evaluation found that nudging enables simulations to progress further without reducing the presence notable dynamics compared to simulations without nudging. A case study with AgentDynEx documented instances where real users were able to simulate lived experiences. We discuss the importance of nudging as a technique for guiding agents towards desirable behaviors while preserving their freedom of choice.

contents.title: Escaping the Nash Trap: Structural Estimation and Alignment of Strategic Reasoning in Large Language Models
contents.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as decision-making agents in competitive and strategic environments, their performance depends critically on how they model human counterparts. Yet little is known about the implicit assumptions LLMs make about human rationality. Drawing on the level-k thinking framework from behavioral game theory, we design a suite of normal-form games and introduce a structural estimation procedure that infers an LLM's latent belief about its opponent’s reasoning depth from observed choices. Across models, we find a systematic bias: LLM agents overwhelmingly assume humans to be Nash-type players, i.e., fully rational strategic optimizers, and respond with equilibrium play. However, human subjects in our online experiments exhibit substantial heterogeneity, spanning \textsc{Random} through \textsc{Nash} reasoning. This mismatch has important consequences. In some settings, an LLM that outsmarts a boundedly rational human secures higher payoffs. In others, however, overestimating human sophistication induces what we term a \emph{Nash equilibrium trap}: equilibrium play yields strictly lower joint payoffs than strategies calibrated to actual human behavior. We propose a behaviorally grounded prompting intervention that explicitly accounts for heterogeneity in human reasoning. This intervention directionally attenuates equilibrium-centric behavior for most models, but its payoff effects are heterogeneous and depend on the model's baseline calibration to human play. Our results demonstrate that strategic competence alone is insufficient for effective human--AI interaction. Accurate modeling of human rationality is a distinct alignment challenge for LLM agents operating in real-world decision-making settings: models must not only move away from rigid equilibrium reasoning when appropriate, but also deviate in ways that are calibrated to observed human behavior.

contents.title: Adapting Socio-Technical Congruence to Human-Agent Collectives
contents.abstract: Socio-technical congruence is the fit between the coordination required by a project's technical dependencies and the coordination its participants actually perform. The construct was developed for human software teams, where assignments are stable, timescales are comparable, channels are observable, and dependencies are code-level. Once AI agents join such collectives, those conditions fail. Existing taxonomies map the design space of human-agent collectives, but do not adapt the dependency-coordination construct itself. We adapt the construct by naming four background assumptions the original construct implicitly relied on, redefining the coordination-requirements matrix over a typed and time-varying actor and dependency graph, and deriving a typology of eight incongruence modes that enumerate the asymmetric ways those assumptions fail. We then specify a generative model of human-agent collectives and use Monte Carlo simulation to derive a parameter-sweep prediction for each incongruence mode. The result is a vocabulary for structural breakdowns in human-agent collectives, with predicted-rate curves as a starting point for empirical work.

blocks.name: Reimagining Scientific Discovery: Collective Intelligence Through the Convergence of Citizen Science and Computational Systems

contents.title: Reimagining Scientific Discovery: Collective Intelligence Through the Convergence of Citizen Science and Computational Systems
contents.abstract: Join a discussion on how we can accelerate scientific discovery through the intentional combination of the speed and scale of modern computational technologies with the reach of distributed publics as a model of collective intelligence grounded in human-machine teaming.

contents.title: MusiChat: Vibe Composing for Music Creation
contents.abstract: Recent advances in AI music generation have enabled users to create complete musical pieces from natural-language prompts. However, most existing systems follow a prompt-and-regenerate paradigm, making iterative refinement difficult because users must repeatedly recreate compositions instead of directly evolving existing musical ideas. We present MusiChat, a conversational vibe composing system that enables collaborative human--AI music creation through natural-language interaction and iterative refinement. At the core of MusiChat is a hierarchical controllable music generation framework that separates lyric-aligned musical structure generation from expressive surface realization, allowing flexible stylistic transformations and structure-preserving edits. The system integrates a large language model with a hybrid symbolic music engine through a memory-augmented architecture that maintains the active composition state and user history across interactions. A hybrid intent-routing mechanism further enables efficient interpretation of both precise musical edits and open-ended creative requests. Rather than regenerating compositions from scratch, MusiChat incrementally transforms an evolving musical artifact while preserving relevant musical structure and user intent. Overall, MusiChat supports coherent multi-turn music authoring and interactive human--AI co-creation through a conversational interface.

contents.title: VibeJam: A User Study Platform for Web Development with Agents
contents.abstract: Programming with AI is increasingly agentic—users prompt LLMs to directly edit their code and review the changes—with adoption growing especially for web development tasks. Despite this growth, most NLP work uses offline evaluation and lacks support for online studies, losing insights into how programmers truly use coding agents. In this demo, we release VibeJam, a browser-based user study platform for users to collaborate with AI agents to develop websites. VibeJam enables agent customization and uses the open-source Aider agent by default, and to mirror downstream use, we add diff review, chat and plan modes, and live website previews. In our supplementary materials, we present a pilot study with 55 released, game-based website creation tasks, where five experienced AI programmers rate our system as fun, simple, and resembling commercial tools, while 13 junior students use VibeJam to make websites of higher quality than agents in the same task. We open-source VibeJam to spur extensions and support studies on how coding agents can help users.

contents.title: BenchMarkerUI: An Interactive System for Auditing and Repairing Multiple-Choice Benchmarks
contents.abstract: Multiple-choice questions are common for evaluating both students and AI models (e.g., LLMs), but they are often riddled with Item Writing Flaws (IWFs) that can confuse test-takers with poor writing practices. To address this, our demonstration presents BenchMarkerUI: a human-AI collaboration tool that uses LLM judges and LLM-generated suggestions to semi-automatically audit and repair MCQs. Our interface includes severity classification, highlighted review, and custom rewriting affordances to improve usefulness and ease of access. In our live demonstration, we plan to have participants bring their own multiple-choice questions or look at existing AI benchmarks to give feedback on our system.

contents.title: A Mobile Tool for Naturalistically Logging Human Information-Seeking Across Search Engines and Conversational AI
contents.abstract: Studies of information-seeking behaviour typically rely on task-based experiments or logs from a single platform, both of which limit ecological validity and generalisability. We present a mobile tool that passively captures organic information-seeking behaviour by analysing on-screen text collected through the AWARE framework. The tool uses regular expressions and platform-specific heuristics to identify search queries on Google, Bing, and Yahoo, as well as prompts entered into ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In a controlled evaluation, the tool correctly identified 93.3% of search queries (42/45) and 82.4% of LLM prompts (14/17). These results show that on-screen text analysis is a viable method for capturing naturalistic information-seeking, and provide a foundation for future work on how people divide information-seeking between search engines and conversational AI in everyday mobile contexts.

contents.title: AI in Information Cascades
contents.abstract: As AI tools become common inputs in economic decisions, public actions become increasingly difficult to interpret. A sequence of identical choices may reflect a cluster of independent data or merely repeated reliance on the same AI signal. This creates a fundamental trade-off: shared AI usage correlates actions and accelerates herding, but it also dilutes the informational value of public histories, pushing decision-makers back to their own private signals. I formalize this trade-off in a BHW-style social learning model where some agents observe a shared AI signal and others receive independent signals. With unobserved agent types, public history endogenously reveals both the state of the world and the underlying sources of past actions. I find that AI transforms social learning in three regimes: low-precision AI exacerbates the risk of incorrect cascades; high-precision AI dictates long-run social outcomes; and intermediate precision induces non-monotonicities, meaning better AI can locally degrade social learning. Together, the results show that evaluating AI by precision alone is incomplete.

contents.title: An Empirical Study on Human Evaluation of Legal Generative AI Applications
contents.abstract: Developing useful and safe generative AI applications for use by technical professionals requires a sound evaluation strategy to ensure outputs meet end-user quality standards. The contributions of this paper are twofold. First, we describe the methodology that we have developed for human evaluation of specific categories of applications with generative AI components. Second, we present a quantitative analysis of the methodology, which was conducted on a dataset with known “gold standard” answers. The analysis demonstrates that the methodology effectively distinguishes between application implementations of differing quality on several useful dimensions.

contents.title: Diamond In The Sky: Towards Human–AI Complementary Story-Driven Learning Environment for Children's STEM Education
contents.abstract: The vast majority of the educational applications developed using the concept of AI mostly focus on providing personalization in learning resources but provide very little collaboration between learners, teachers, and the AI system. In this paper, we present our work on "Diamond In The Sky," an ongoing project where we are building an educational game powered by AI and exploring the possibility of collaborative learning between humans and AI systems in STEM education for children using a game-based narrative approach and adaptive AI help systems. Our game prototype uses the power of story-telling, adaptive missions, adaptivity, and learner development using React, TypeScript, Supabase, and the OpenAI API. Unlike other educational applications that have been developed using AI to replace the teacher, our application aims to collaborate with the teacher.

contents.title: Dynamic Complementarity in Human–LLM Collaboration: Modeling Competence Evolution Over Repeated Decision Tasks
contents.abstract: Human-AI complementarity is usually evaluated on a fixed set of tasks: does the combined system outperform either working alone? This view is incomplete when people work with large language models (LLMs) across a sequence of related, repeated tasks. In such settings, LLMs can improve performance on a given task within a sequence, while also changing human competence, defined as the ability to perform tasks independently and to evaluate, verify, or correct LLM outputs. We call this temporal perspective "dynamic complementarity." It evaluates a collaboration pattern by its performance over a task sequence and by the changes in human competence. We instantiate the idea in a stylized simulation model in which repeated collaboration affects both task outcomes and human competence. The model separates two effects that are often collapsed in prior static complementarity models: (i) how collaboration affects the outputs produced during the sequence, and (ii) how it changes the human who will participate in subsequent tasks. This separation shows why human–LLM complementarity behaves differently across collaboration patterns with different assumptions about how competence changes. Dynamic complementarity provides a conceptual foundation to study human-LLM systems in the context of repeated collaborations.

contents.title: Exploration vs. Fixation: Scaffolding Divergent and Convergent Thinking for Human-AI Co-Creation with Generative Models
contents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used for open-ended creative tasks such as story writing, product design, and video creation. However, popular chatbot-based interfaces often prioritize execution, generating fully rendered outputs right away. This can lead to premature convergence and design fixation, where users are anchored to initial outputs. Recent work has proposed new interfaces to address this issue by supporting exploration, though typically constrained to be semantically close to a user's initial task framing, potentially limiting the creativity of the outcomes. We examine an approach for human-AI co-creation and instantiate it in HAICo, a system for image co-creation. HAICo structures the creative process into two switchable modes: DIVERGENT mode supports users in exploration by surfacing remote conceptual ideas that users might not reach on their own, while CONVERGENT mode supports users in aligning model outputs with their refinement intent through generating intent interpretations surfaced as options. Through a within-subjects study on a poster image creation task, we demonstrate that HAICo outperforms ChatGPT across multiple dimensions of creativity and usability. Our results highlight the potential of leveraging human-AI complementarity to expand the exploration space and treating alignment as an interactive process through which user intent is interpreted and progressively specified.

contents.title: Human-AI Co-Construction of Verifiable Narrative Identity: A Pilot Study on Family Stories
contents.abstract: To address the vulnerability of personal narratives and support a more verifiable form of narrative identity, we propose a small-scale, high-context Human–AI workflow in which AI decomposes narratives into claims and routes uncertain cases, while family members verify evidence and preserve disagreement. A pilot study involving five family participants investigates whether this workflow yields scalable yet verifiable narrative identity.

contents.title: Human-AI Collaboration for Detecting AI-Generated Media: Just-in-Time Advice from Experts and LLMs
contents.abstract: AI-generated images and videos now circulate widely, and people struggle to tell them from real media. Automated detectors do not solve this problem, because they are not robust: each new generative model can be trained to evade the last classifier, and everyday transformations such as compression, cropping, and local edits degrade them further. A more robust approach helps people evaluate media for themselves. We test whether just-in-time advice, delivered while a person makes a judgment, produces human-AI complementarity, in which a person and an AI system together detect AI-generated media better than either alone. We ran a preregistered experiment with 2,699 participants across nine stimulus sets of people, spanning photographs and videos that vary in pose, resolution, occupation, provenance, geopolitical context, and generative-model vintage. We randomly assigned every judgment to one of three conditions: a control nudge, advice from a frontier LLM that did not know the ground truth, or advice from a human expert. The advice never revealed the answer. It directed attention to specific visual features. We find that expert advice increases detection of AI-generated media by 7.1 percentage points, and that expert advice outperforms LLM advice on synthetic images by 2.7 percentage points. Advice also raises false positives on real images: it pushes participants toward "fake" responses, so authentic images are more often mislabeled as AI-generated. Because each participant judges a sequence of stimuli, we study how this complementarity evolves over the course of interaction and whether it holds as generative models advance. These results show that just-in-time advice can improve human detection.

contents.title: Human-AI Collaborative Ontology Editing: An LLM-Assisted Dashboard for Improving an Ontology of Work Activities
contents.abstract: Ontology editing is an open-ended task: there is rarely a predefined standard for the single correct structure, and appropriate representations emerge only as the work unfolds. We present a human-in-the-loop dashboard for improving the Work Nouns Ontology from the MIT Ontology of Work Activities, a ~3,300-node hierarchy derived from O*NET containing five recurring error types. In our system, the LLM proposes edits with explanations. Reviewers accept, modify, or reject them, and their decisions are distilled into editing principles that update future prompts. In a five-participant think-aloud study, reviewers made 119 decisions, accepting 58.0% of suggestions overall, but acceptance ranged from 78.3% for duplicates to 15.8% for incorrect multiple parents. A post-hoc active-learning experiment shows reviewer decisions contain learnable patterns. We find AI assistance is most effective for localized edits with relatively objective answers, while broader structural decisions still require human judgment.

contents.title: Human-AI Complementarity in Poverty Governance: An Interpretable XGBoost Scorecard for Calibrating Human Decision-Making
contents.abstract: Poverty targeting in developing nations relies on Proxy Means Tests (PMTs) built via stepwise logistic regression and subjective variable selection—a process prone to bias and instability. While XGBoost eliminates these flaws and improves accuracy, its opacity makes it unsuitable for pencil-and-paper field deployment or the calibrated human trust that high-stakes governance requires. To achieve algorithmic objectivity without sacrificing human interpretability, this paper develops two intrinsically explainable poverty scorecards. We employ XGBoost across 500 bootstrap samples to identify 11 stable high-gain predictors from 120 candidates, treating district as a geographic control and using the remaining 10 household-level predictors to construct interpretable scorecards, removing subjective human intervention entirely from the feature-selection phase. We then construct two interpretable scoring instruments: Scorecard 1 (Logistic Regression Scorecard, LRS), whose point weights are derived from logistic regression coefficients applied to the XGBoost-selected features, and Scorecard 2 (XGBoost Scorecard, XGBS), whose weights are derived directly from XGBoost's feature information gain, providing a transparent Explainable AI (XAI) translation of the model's internal logic. Both scorecards are evaluated against the full 120-feature XGBoost model and a reduced 10-feature XGBoost model to quantify the cost of transparency. Scorecard 1 achieves 75.0% accuracy (AUC = 0.833), within 1.2 percentage points of the full black-box model (76.2%), while Scorecard 2 (AUC = 0.755, 66.1% accuracy) captures complex non-linear poverty dynamics in a human-readable form. By deliberately separating AI-driven feature extraction from human-led threshold selection, this work operationalizes a principled division of labor: the algorithm handles high-dimensional statistical ranking, while policymakers retain full agency over the ethical trade-offs between undercoverage and leakage. This research contributes both a practical targeting tool for social safety net programs and a replicable methodology for bridging algorithmic power and human interpretability in high-stakes societal governance.

contents.title: Mapping AI Exposure Across the U.S. Workforce: Evidence from Millions of AI Conversations
contents.abstract: Having accurate measures of how the workforce is exposed to AI is vital for policymakers planning intervention, educators redesigning curriculum, businesses deciding how to adapt, and researchers understanding how to produce more and better research. Many studies contain incomplete measurement on what economic work AI can perform. We create a composite exposure dataset by combining AI usage data from Anthropic's Claude (browser and API) and Microsoft's Copilot with occupational data from O*NET and employment and wage data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Overall, we measure that 29.3% of economy-wide tasks are currently exposed with an annual growth rate of 48.7%. Exposure converges on occupational sectors of Computer and Math, Sales, Business, Office and Administration, and Education. These findings provide detailed signals for directing policy, education, the workforce, and research toward the areas of greatest transformation from AI.

contents.title: Preserving the Record of a Cultural Computing Community: A Human-AI Collaborative Knowledge Graph Workflow
contents.abstract: This project presents a human-AI collaborative knowledge graph workflow for identifying and querying digital preservation risks in three Laptop Orchestra of Louisiana compositions recovered from two legacy MacBook Pros. The workflow combines archivist-created piece records with locally extracted file and dependency evidence in a Neo4j graph aligned with the CIDOC Conceptual Reference Model (CIDOC CRM). Local computational extraction structures technical evidence from Max patch files, while LLM-supported tools process piece records and support natural-language querying. The pilot demonstrates how practitioner review can guide the use of LLM-supported tools and knowledge graph methods to integrate archival and technical evidence for digital preservation.

contents.title: Supporting Personal Investigative Sensemaking with an Emotion-Adaptive AI Assistant
contents.abstract: Traditional technological support for sensemaking takes a cognitive perspective while largely ignoring people's struggles with complex emotional landscapes. In this paper, we introduce the concept of personal investigative sensemaking and a novel browser-based software tool, Genet, that provides behavioral guardrails and LLM-powered emotion-adaptive sensemaking support to amateur genealogists. We conducted a field experiment evaluating this system over two weeks with 12 amateur genealogists. Our findings reveal how the system affected participants' sensemaking and experiences, and shed light on how AI-powered sensemaking support could be integrated to facilitate complex sensemaking with diverse user profiles, sensemaking tasks, and information sources.

contents.title: Trusted but Untouched: How Opacity and Audience Distance Stall Synthetic Interview Outputs Before Collective Sensemaking
contents.abstract: Whether AI-generated research artifacts strengthen a team's collective sensemaking depends on more than their fidelity: people must be able to steer what the AI produces, and the outputs must be credible enough to circulate beyond who generated them. Five UX practitioners in one industry organization used a staged synthetic interview tool with three human-in-the-loop checkpoints and reflected on how they would position and share its outputs. Sharing declined with audience distance, and although reviewing built trust, four of five avoided editing, citing uncertainty about how edits would propagate. We discuss edit-propagation previews and audience-matched artifact forms as conditions for AI outputs to reach collective sensemaking.

contents.title: What Should Humans Refuse to Delegate to AI? A Turing Test for Civilization
contents.abstract: Human-AI research often asks how tasks should be divided between humans and machines; this talk asks which human roles should not be delegated at all. Alan Turing's imitation game asked whether a machine could convincingly perform as human. The question now is whether human communities can identify which forms of human work should remain human, even when machines can perform them well. This talk proposes a Turing Test for Civilization: a framework for distinguishing tasks that may be automated, tasks that should be assisted, and activities that should remain meaningfully human. I call the third category non-delegable human work. These are activities whose value reaches past their output to human responsibility, formation, relational presence, ritual meaning, and public legitimacy. The talk applies the framework to education, caregiving, democratic judgment, creative work, and mourning. In each case, AI may generate useful outputs, but human participation remains part of the good being protected. The contribution is a vocabulary for human-AI complementarity that moves beyond performance substitution toward purpose-preserving design.

contents.title: Engineering Predictable Turing Patterns for Spatial Organisation in Swarm Robotics
contents.abstract: Biologically inspired reaction-diffusion (Turing) equations can serve as a. decentralised tool to create varying spatial patterns across robots in a swarm. The ability to systematically engineer such patterns is the basis of morphodynamic engineering in robot swarms and enables applications in spatial task allocation, swarm connectivity and within construction and self-assembly. In this paper, a design methodology is established for selecting parameters to control the peak growth rate and dominant Turing mode characterising the patterns that arise from the underlying reaction-diffusion model. As demonstrated in both simulations and physical experiments on Kilobots, we show that the system can be tuned for desired spatial wavelength despite the heterogeneities present in Kilobot swarms, as evidenced in both regular and irregular formations.

contents.title: Communication Heterogeneity and Collective Consensus in Neural Cellular Automata
contents.abstract: Reaching global agreement from purely local interactions is a defining problem of collective intelligence, and most models of it assume that all agents share a single communication protocol. We ask what happens when they do not. Using a Neural Cellular Automaton in which a population of cells must solve the density classification task, agreeing on a global majority that no individual can observe, we introduce “languages” as sub-populations that read one another’s messages through a translation with a tunable “linguistic distance”. We find that linguistic distance slows consensus, that it produces mild divergence between groups rather than full fragmentation, and that a collective whose shared rule was trained under diverse protocols is robust to mismatch; a homogeneously trained one is not. The findings hold on both a ring and a two-dimensional grid, and admit a natural reading as Ising relaxation, in which a foreign-language region acts as a boundary defect that leaves the system in a higher-energy, partially ordered state. These patterns are qualitatively consistent with effects reported in human group studies, suggesting that distance between communication protocols is a minimal mechanism sufficient to produce them, without anything language-specific.

contents.title: Same Structure, Different Trajectories: Community Dissolution on an AI Agent Social Platform
contents.abstract: As large language models become widely adopted, agent-only social platforms have begun to emerge on the public internet. Moltbook, currently the largest general-purpose agent-only platform, hosts tens of thousands of LLM agents in a Reddit-like infrastructure with posts, comments, voting, and topic-based communities, but unlike human platforms, only agents can post. We ask how collective behavior in LLM agent communities differs from human communities, and why. Matching 12 Moltbook communities with 12 topically similar subreddits over a 29-day window, we find a process we call Community Dissolution: topic boundaries erode, interaction patterns lose distinctiveness, and signals of valued contribution nearly disappear. We link these patterns to two agent-level limitations: output homogenization and a norm enforcement deficit in which agents accommodate rather than challenge violations.

contents.title: A Cognitive Account of Density Effects in Highly-Interdependent Networks
contents.abstract: Collective performance depends on both the structure of social interaction and the cognitive demands of the task. Network structure shapes how groups search, learn, coordinate, and converge on solutions–dense networks can accelerate the diffusion of successful solutions, but they can also encourage exploitation of safe options, reducing the diversity needed to discover better solutions [2, 10, 12]. Research on coordination and cooperation similarly shows that local interaction, repeated encounters, and information about others’ actions and outcomes influence coordination [4, 8, 11, 14]. Prior collaboration ties can also be critical for performance in naturalistic settings [7, 9]. Current literature establishes that network structure influences collective outcomes, but it does not fully explain the cognitive mechanisms producing these effects. One determinant of cognitive demands is interdependence: the extent to which individuals’ outcomes depend on their own actions and those of others [1, 13]. Under low interdependence, individuals can learn successful behavior primarily from their own choices and outcomes. Under high interdependence, success requires adapting to others’ behavior, making network density more consequential. Although repeated interactions within fixed pairings in sparse networks can facilitate coordination, and changing partners can impede it [3],it remains unclear whether density impairs coordination because individuals have fewer experiences with each partner or because experiences with different partners interfere when adaptation must be partner-specific. We provide a cognitive account of how network density affects collective coordination using Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT; [6]). We propose that diverse interaction partners in dense networks create interference among experiences, hindering convergence when successful behavior requires partner-specific adaptation. This account predicts that density should have little effect when rewards are independent of the partner but impair coordination under high interdependence. This prediction is verified in an experiment involving low and high interdependent contexts and three network structures: disconnected dyads, lattice networks, and fully connected networks. We then provide novel predictions using an IBL model that represents partner identity [5] to suggest that the density effect diminishes when agents can discriminate partner-specific interaction histories.

contents.title: Implicit Physical Coordination as a Group-Level Trait: Preliminary Evidence from Youth Football
contents.abstract: When scouts look for the next football star, they typically focus on individual skill and athleticism. But what makes a team actually win often goes beyond any person’s individual contributions. It's about a team's collective coordination (CC). This study explored whether that quality (CC), can be intuited by coaches and used to predict performance in youth football. Working with U11 and U12 players across three field studies, we asked coaches to intuitively group players by their anticipated teamwork. We then validated these groupings by having the teams compete in short, non-football, non-verbal coordination tasks. High CC teams consistently outperformed lower CC groups, completing the coordination tasks 52.8% faster on average, winning during tactical training drills and small-sided games. This suggests that CC can be assessed efficiently before teams touch a ball, and this metric could be a practical, identifiable metric for youth player development, though larger studies are needed to confirm these findings.

blocks.name: Human Computation in the Age of AI

contents.title: Measuring Proof Burden in Public Bounty Listings: A RentAHuman Case Study
contents.abstract: Online bounty markets let requesters advertise paid tasks to workers. A worker may be asked not only to complete a task but also to prove that it was completed, and proving can mean exposure: revealing identity or location, using a personal account, posting publicly, acting in the physical world, or supplying evidence again during later checks—none disclosed by the posted price. We call these advertised requirements proof burden and measure them on RentAHuman, a 2026 market publicized as a place where AI agents could hire humans. We study what listings request, not what workers submit or experience. We manually audited a nonrandom May 31, 2026 snapshot: every listing our searches returned from RentAHuman and Human Pages, another such market—981 listings, all but one from RentAHuman. Two independent coders recorded 13 features—11 kinds of evidence, recurring monitoring (repeated checks), and physical-world action—and our 0–5 Proof Burden Score; a blinded third coder resolved every disagreement. A planned content screen leaves 779 bounty/task listings as the primary population; among them, physical-world action appears in 48.5%, photo proof in 37.1%, and identity proof in 30.9%, and 438 listings (56.2%) score 4 or 5. Those listings span 154 distinct feature combinations: a checklist, not a single score, tells workers what a listing entails. Platform metadata labels some requester accounts as agents or bots. In exploratory comparisons, physical-world action, location proof, or recurring monitoring appeared in 75.0% of agent-or-bot-labeled versus 55.3% of human-labeled listings, while their score-4-or-5 shares did not clearly differ. The labels are self-reported or platform-assigned, the agent-or-bot-labeled listings come from only 20 displayed names, and the comparison was chosen after seeing the data: a hypothesis, not a confirmed difference. Our main contributions are the 13-requirement vocabulary, the adjudicated manual audit, and the descriptive case study of this market; the score is a secondary screening summary, and the requester-label comparison exploratory. The study offers no worker-validated measure or automated detector yet; it is groundwork for both.

contents.title: Guiding Worker Self-Selection in Crowdsourcing Contests: An LLM-Augmented Algorithmic Approach
contents.abstract: Crowdsourcing platforms coordinate large pools of online workers who compete in contests to produce solutions for clients, from logo design to machine-learning challenges. A defining feature of these platforms is that workers self-select: Each chooses which contests to enter and how much effort to invest, and these choices are strategic rather than aligned with what the platform needs. As a result, the platform may end up with too few participants, or too little effort, on the contests where high-quality solutions matter most—while individual workers may end up dissatisfied, regretting choices that left them worse off than an alternative they could have taken. To reconcile these competing interests, platforms increasingly offer workers recommendations on where to compete. We study how to generate such recommendations as the game of self-selection in Tullock contests (SSTC), a two-stage model in which workers first choose contests and then compete within them. We introduce GRAF, a greedy algorithmic framework that produces self-selection outcomes in polynomial time by ordering workers according to a score vector, with provable guarantees—zero worker regret and platform optimality—for special cases of SSTC. Because a good ordering is difficult to design by hand once workers are heterogeneous, we propose LLMScore, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that automatically designs the scoring algorithm GRAF uses. LLMScore addresses two obstacles to applying existing LLM-based methods here: jointly optimizing solution quality and worker satisfaction, and the intractability of evaluating worker regret. It is trained only on small instances of a single setting yet transfers to larger and structurally different settings, and—because its output is human-readable code—a platform operator can inspect and adjust the recommendation logic it learns. Across 1,000 synthetic instances spanning four settings, GRAF augmented by LLMScore consistently yields near-optimal outcomes with low worker regret, benefiting platform and workers alike.

contents.title: Looks Can be Deceiving: Annotator and Reviewer Performance Across Imagery Scales In Aerial Damage Assessment
contents.abstract: This paper presents the first known empirical investigation of annotator and reviewer performance across multi-source remotely sensed imagery, evaluating human labeling across drone, crewed aviation, and satellite views. Because existing aerial imagery datasets rely predominantly on single-source imagery, there is currently no established state of practice for efficiently allocating human labor to curate large-scale, multi-scale aerial datasets. This work addresses this limitation by analyzing annotator performance within a post-disaster building damage assessment dataset of 9 disasters, where 20,041 buildings in drone, 20,695 buildings in crewed aviation, and 33,392 buildings in satellite imagery were labeled. These labels, provided by 187 annotators, were evaluated by comparing two distinct quality-control strategies: a single-reviewer pass versus a consensus-committee review. Our analysis reveals two surprising findings that challenge standard crowd-sourcing practices. First, annotator error rates scale as image resolution decreases with p<4.45x10^-12 (6.85% for drone, 25.52% for crewed aviation, and 38.07% for satellite), showing consistently higher error rates across all stages of labeling workflow. Second, relying on a single reviewer is insufficient to maintain annotation quality, often leaving substantial errors for the consensus committee to correct. This demonstrates that uniformly allocating human reviewer capacity across multi-source datasets is highly inefficient and results in severe label disagreement in lower-resolution imagery. To mitigate these risks to human-AI complementarity systems, this paper offers three recommendations for dataset curation in order to train and evaluate downstream computer vision models that complement human-AI systems in societal settings like disaster response: (1) tailor labeling schemas directly to imagery resolution, (2) prioritize consensus-based review mechanisms over individual reviews, and (3) disproportionately target quality-control efforts toward lower-resolution imagery.

contents.title: The Polymath Plus Project: AI-mediated human collaboration to advance mathematical discovery
contents.abstract: PolyPlus is an online collaboration platform that combines large-scale human participation with AI-based reasoning to advance mathematical discovery. This work builds on the successes and challenges [1][2] of the original Polymath project [3], an experiment in crowd-sourced mathematical problem solving, which famously yielded a simplified proof of the Density Hales–Jewett theorem. Our approach leverages AI in two ways: as an administrator that manages discussion threads and provides contextual summaries to users who want understand the current state of a proof, and as a collaborator that contributes new ideas and serves as a conversational intermediary between human mathematicians and a formal proof verification system. By uniting human intuition with machine-assisted rigor, PolyPlus aims to produce simpler proofs of established theorems, tackle unsolved challenges, and extend the benefits of AI-enhanced collaboration to a broader mathematical community.

contents.title: Qualification by Calibration: A Readable Benchmark for Admitting Language Models to Human-Computation Tasks
contents.abstract: When several language models are wired together into a pipeline, the system routes, arbitrates, and escalates based on how confident each model says it is. That makes trust calibration, the agreement between a model's stated confidence and how often it is actually right, the measurement on which the whole arrangement depends. Crowdsourcing has long screened human contributors with small qualification tests of gold-answer questions before admitting them to a task; a team builder who wants to apply the same discipline to a candidate language model, checking its calibration before admitting it to a pipeline, has no comparably small and inspectable instrument. We present one: a compact benchmark of yes or no questions across five everyday domains, each item marked easy or hard, on which a model reports both an answer and a confidence. We evaluate four contemporary models and find that the panel cleanly separates a poorly calibrated model from well calibrated ones: its accuracy interval sits far below and apart from the others, and its most confident answers are its least accurate, a separation that a single well calibrated model alone would hide. We treat the gold answers as part of the contribution and verify every item against authoritative sources, correcting one error this surfaced. The benchmark is deliberately small so that a deployer can run and read it in full; we discuss what such an instrument can and cannot establish at this size, and release the items, the model responses, and the scoring code so that the check becomes a single command rather than a project.

contents.title: Human-AI Collaboration: Building Agents That Augment Work
contents.abstract: AI agents are transforming how people work; however, building agents that augment workers requires knowing what they want from AI, how they collaborate with it, and whether that collaboration helps them. In this talk, we first audit the U.S. workforce to map where workers want automation, where they want augmentation, and where AI capabilities fall short, complemented by an analysis of nearly 250,000 real-world conversations. We then introduce frameworks to measure collaboration directly by pairing workers with agents on real-world tasks to separate human and agent skill contributions, and by quantifying how much cognitive effort users offload through reconstructing how they would have worked without AI. Overall, this talk highlights how to understand and evaluate human-AI collaboration and how to design agents that augment human work.

contents.title: Workshop Reports

blocks.name: How Open Practices Shape Collective Intelligence

contents.title: How Open Practices Shape Collective Intelligence
contents.abstract: Many people believe that openness improves science, software production, government, and other collective efforts. But how true is this? And what is "openness" anyway? This session will share findings from new reports and field experts on open practices. Panelists will discuss how open practices can help and hurt collective intelligence, both within science specifically and across many types of organizations more generally.

blocks.name: Human Judgment, Trust, and Learning with AI

contents.title: One AI Signal, Many Human Judgments: A Bayesian Cascade Analysis of AI-based Credibility Indicators in Online Information Spread
contents.abstract: Social media platforms increasingly use AI-based credibility indicators to help users judge misinformation. Unlike individual human-AI decision-making, these indicators are embedded in information spread: users see both an AI prediction and earlier judgments shaped by the same AI, and their own judgments may then enter the public history. Yet how to analytically characterize this process remains under-explored. We therefore introduce a social-learning lens for this setting by extending the classical Bayesian cascade model with the AI indicator as a shared public signal. The resulting Gateway condition compares the evidence from the AI prediction with users' private impressions. Through this view, we show that AI changes what public history means. Crowd agreement may reflect accumulated independent human evidence, or repeated dependence on the same AI prediction. This creates a preservation-correction trade-off: stronger reliance on AI can preserve correct predictions, but can also lock in incorrect ones by blocking corrective private impressions. We calibrate the model using human-subject data on news veracity judgments. Although the AI outperforms human users, the average user weights it below her own impression but above several peer judgments, while individual users vary from discounting the AI to relying on it enough to cascade. Simulations show that over-reliance on a weak AI is especially harmful, and that diversifying AI signals across users can better keep the crowd informative. We conclude with implications for understanding human-AI interaction in information spread and designing misinformation interventions.

contents.title: The Belief Update Gate: Separating Inertia from Learning in Human–AI Interaction
contents.abstract: Repeated human-AI interaction is often analyzed through pooled belief-updating slopes: users observe AI successes and failures, revise beliefs in the feedback-consistent direction, but appear conservative on average. We argue that this average hides a more granular phenomenon, which we call the "belief update gate": before asking how strongly people update, we must first ask whether feedback changes their reported belief at all. Reanalyzing a multi-task human-AI decision-making dataset with 240 participants, 7,200 trials, and three task domains, we find that user-reported beliefs often do not measurably move: 67.3% of trial-level belief changes are exactly zero, and 76.4% are smaller than five percentage points. When non-moving reports are separated from reports that change, the apparent conservatism in pooled updating is substantially reduced: the within-trajectory slope rises from 0.494 overall to 0.949 among rows with nonzero movement. Complementary hurdle-style analyses show the same pattern: the discrepancy between feedback and entering belief predicts whether a report changes, while feedback direction predicts the size and direction of change among reports that move. These findings suggest that belief formation in repeated human-AI interaction is better understood as two linked processes: whether feedback produces a measurable change in reported belief, and how reported beliefs change conditional on movement. More broadly, calibration analyses should distinguish non-movement in elicited belief reports, conditional learning, and coarse or rounded reporting rather than treating reported beliefs as a single continuous updating process.

contents.title: Easy to Read, Easy to Trust: How Processing Fluency in LLM Explanations Drives Over-Reliance in Hate Speech Moderation
contents.abstract: This study examines the challenges human moderators face in AI-assisted detection of online hate speech, particularly when discriminatory intent is conveyed through implicit or nuanced language. Following the Judge-Advisor System (JAS) paradigm, we evaluate how different types of Large Language Model (LLM)-generated explanations support human moderators in hate speech detection. We hypothesized that natural language explanations would offer more interpretable rationales, helping moderators better assess the accuracy of AI recommendations and make informed decisions that reflect appropriate reliance on AI. Contrary to this expectation, our results show that explanation form does not affect decision accuracy but significantly reshapes reliance: fluent natural language explanations heighten moderators' over-reliance on the AI—leading them to follow it even when it errs—whereas feature-based explanations promote scrutiny and self-reliance. We interpret this phenomenon through the lens of processing fluency within the meta-reasoning framework. Drawing on these cognitive science insights and the observed variation in how moderators process different explanation types, we provide practical design suggestions for AI-assisted moderation tools and call for greater cross-disciplinary engagement in future HCI research on human-AI decision-making.

contents.title: Cognitive Security for Human-AI Systems
contents.abstract: As generative and agentic AI systems become embedded in search, education, productivity, companionship, social media, and decision support, trust and safety risks increasingly arise from how AI systems shape attention, belief formation, memory, judgment, agency, and trust, well beyond the content of any single model output. This talk proposes cognitive security as a field-building frame for human-AI systems: the study and mitigation of recurring vulnerabilities in the cognitive conditions that allow people and groups to reason independently. We present an emerging cognitive-security agenda organized around three questions. First, what cognitive capacities should human-AI systems be expected to protect, among them attention, belief formation and judgment, memory and provenance, and agency? Second, what repeatable vulnerability patterns arise across AI-mediated environments, grouped by the cognitive capacity they target: attention (epistemic flooding), belief formation and judgment (fluency overtrust, authority transfer), memory and provenance (context collapse), and agency (automation deference, emotional dependency, agentic misalignment)? Third, what institutional infrastructure is needed to translate these risks into product review, red teaming, incident reporting, researcher access, audit checklists, and future standards? The contribution is a broader framework for taking cognitive security from principle to practice. Beyond naming harms, it consolidates a scattered vocabulary into a shared one, anchored in the Cognitive Vulnerability and Mitigation Catalog (CVMC). The CVMC is a structured schema that pairs each AI affordance and cognitive vulnerability with a candidate mitigation, an evaluation metric, a burden-and-equity check, and a governance hook, so that each recurring pattern becomes a trackable entry with a stable identifier. The aim is a shared vocabulary, mitigation catalogue, and governance agenda for preserving independent judgment in AI-mediated environments.

contents.title: Adaptive Selection of Effective AI Assistance in AI-assisted Decision Making Using Multi-Armed Bandits
contents.abstract: In AI-assisted decision-making, how to present AI assistance significantly influences human cognition, leading to varied reliance strategies when facing different tasks. Current human-AI interaction designs often constrain decision makers to interact with specified default forms of AI assistance, rather than providing personalized, intelligent support that adapts to individual needs across various scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a human-adaptive AI interaction framework for AI-assisted decision-making, which embeds with a multi-armed bandit approach to identify the most effective forms of AI assistance for individuals based on their prior interaction history. Results from a between-subjects experiment across two types of decision making tasks show that our framework promoted more appropriate human trust in AI compared to other default forms of AI assistance. We conclude by discussing the limitations and design implications of our findings for AI-assisted decision making.
