contents.title: How AI Assistance Affects Human Skill Development: A Study of Learning with Logic Puzzles
contents.abstract: While AI assistance can improve human task performance in the short term, it may also undermine the development of skills in the longer term. We examine this tension in a controlled logic-puzzle experiment involving on-demand AI assistance, where participants complete tasks and are assessed both before and after AI is available. By varying AI request costs, we find that lower-cost assistance induces more frequent AI use. We also find that participants who request AI assistance during the AI-access phase perform worse after assistance is removed, and their subsequent unassisted performance is overestimated from earlier AI-assisted performance. We use a Bayesian latent ability model to separate initial ability, post-AI ability, and participant-specific skill change, while estimating how independent reasoning during the AI-access phase relates to skill development. The results show that greater independent problem-solving effort is associated with larger skill gains, suggesting that AI assistance is detrimental to learning primarily when it substitutes for independent reasoning.

contents.title: BirdsongChat: Cross-Modal Generation and Interactive Control for Bird Motion and Soundscape
contents.abstract: We present BirdsongChat, a real-time interactive system for cross-modal generation of bird motion and soundscapes. The system enables users to generate and iteratively refine coordinated avian behaviors using text and image inputs, supporting controllable interaction over attributes such as emotion, species characteristics, and environmental context. BirdsongChat produces synchronized motion and spatialized soundscapes through a modular architecture consisting of a reasoning module, a coordination module, and execution modules for motion and audio generation. A foundation model interprets multimodal inputs and produces structured control signals, which are then executed by specialized modules to generate temporally aligned motion and soundscape outputs in real time. Overall, BirdsongChat demonstrates how interactive multimodal systems can support real-time exploration of coordinated motion and spatial soundscapes, enabling more controllable and expressive generative experiences while maintaining strong alignment between motion and soundscapes and supporting stable interactive control in multi-bird and varied environmental settings.

contents.title: Collective Intelligence Simulator: An Interactive Testbed for Studying Team Decisions Across Agile Sprints
contents.abstract: We demonstrate an interactive testbed that models agile software team process as a collective-intelligence (CI) process across multiple sprints. Collective intelligence— social sensitivity, skills properly managed, and participation balance in terms of collective memory, shared attention, shared reasoning— yet it drives how teams plan, allocate, and adapt. Our tool makes these subconstructs adjustable levers: a researcher moves them, and secondarily adjusts AI decision support and its trust calibration, then watches velocity, defect rate, decision quality, and Hackman-style team effectiveness respond sprint by sprint. We assume that CI can be decomposed into collective memory, shared attention, and shared reasoning. It supports single scenarios, Monte Carlo replication, and one-parameter sensitivity sweeps. Every weight and formula is externalized and inspectable, so the demo is an invitation to interrogate assumptions rather than trust a black box.

contents.title: A taxonomy of rater disagreements: Surveying challenges & opportunities from the perspective of annotating online toxicity
contents.abstract: Toxicity is an increasingly severe issue in online spaces. Consequently, a rich line of research has focused on computationally detecting online toxicity. These efforts crucially rely on human-annotated datasets for training toxicity detection models. However, human annotations in this domain yield low inter-rater agreement. Recent research has pointed out the importance of accounting for the subjective nature of this task, and this has triggered work on understanding rater disagreements. While these efforts are filling an important gap, there is a lack of a comprehensive framework about the root causes of rater disagreement, and therefore, we situate this work within that broader landscape. In this paper, we discuss a wide variety of reasons behind rater disagreements when completing toxicity annotation tasks, and propose a detailed taxonomy for the same. Further, we summarize and discuss potential solutions targeting each reason for disagreement. We also discuss several open issues within online toxicity research.

contents.title: Anchored Sequential Deliberation: Slower Convergence, More Stable Outcomes
contents.abstract: Sequential deliberation is a simple mechanism for collective decision making: repeatedly select a small group of participants, let them deliberate over the current outcome, and use their (dis)agreement as the reference for the next round. Existing theoretical work by Fain et al.~\cite{fain2017sequential} treats the current outcome purely as a disagreement alternative for bargaining. In practice, however, the current outcome is often an existing draft, policy, or proposal that also acts as an \emph{anchor}: participants may not bargain directly from their ideal positions (bliss points), but from stances partially pulled toward the status quo. We study this effect on a one-dimensional decision space and propose a model of anchored sequential deliberation. In each round, two participants with bliss points $U$ and $V$ are selected; they form anchored stances $\Util = (1-\lambda) U + \lambda O_{t-1}$ and $\Vtil = (1-\lambda) V + \lambda O_{t-1}$, where $O_{t-1}$ is the outcome from the previous round and larger $\lambda$ indicates stronger anchoring, and then conduct Nash bargaining with $O_{t-1}$ as the disagreement alternative. Our analysis reveals a trade-off. On the one hand, stronger anchoring slows down convergence: through a coupling of two random walks of the deliberative outcome, we show that the process contracts at rate $\frac{1+\lambda}{2}$. On the other hand, stronger anchoring concentrates the stationary outcome around a \emph{deliberative fixed point}, the point at which the expected movement of the deliberative outcome is zero. For symmetric population distributions, this fixed point coincides with the population median, indicating a better deliberation result. We complement the analysis with simulations on multiple Beta distributions, which empirically show smaller distortion under stronger anchoring.

contents.title: Beyond Consensus: Designing AI Summaries That Preserve Dissent in Group Decision-Making
contents.abstract: While AI-generated summaries are influencing how decision-makers perceive collective opinions, conciseness might result in the omission of rare yet significant perspectives. To address this, we present Dissent-Preserving Summaries (DPS), a structured presentation that distinguishes between consensus, majority opinions, minority perspectives, and open issues, tying claims to their sources. In addition, we recommend conducting a human subjects study that compares typical, frequency-based, and dissent-preserving summaries using group decision situations with valid and invalid minority opinions. Measures used in evaluating the summaries include viewpoint recollection, accuracy, identification of open issues, decision reversal, perceived fairness, mental workload, and false balance.

contents.title: Beyond the Traceback: Crowdsourced Calibration of Skill-Targeted LLM Explanations for Programming Errors
contents.abstract: Programming error messages are a central feedback channel in software development, yet they often remain difficult to interpret and act on, especially for less experienced programmers. Large language models offer a promising way to rewrite such messages into clearer and more actionable explanations, but it remains unclear whether more readable explanations actually improve debugging performance, or how explanation styles should be matched to programmer skill. We present a multi-stage crowdsourced study of skill-targeted, LLM-generated programming error messages for Python. First, we develop and pilot a short debugging-oriented proficiency assessment to classify participants by assessed skill. Second, we use a formative study to curate buggy Python snippets and corresponding interpreter errors across varying difficulty levels. Third, in a study with 103 participants, we compare standard Python interpreter messages with two LLM-generated explanation styles: pragmatic messages, which provide concise action-oriented guidance, and contingent messages, which provide more scaffolded explanatory support. We measure objective debugging outcomes, including fix rate, attempts, and time-to-fix, alongside perceived readability, cognitive load, and tone. LLM-rewritten messages yielded more favorable subjective evaluations, with pragmatic messages rated as clearer, more helpful, and less cognitively demanding than standard interpreter messages. However, these subjective gains did not reliably translate into statistically significant improvements in objective debugging performance. Our results reveal a human-AI complementarity gap in programming support: explanations that feel better to users may not necessarily help them debug more effectively. We discuss implications for designing skill-targeted AI feedback systems, arguing that static explanation rewriting may be insufficient and that future systems should adapt to users’ interaction state, error context, and repair trajectory rather than skill category alone.

contents.title: Dynamic Opinion-policy Feedback Model Explains Long-Term Patterns of Public Opinion Change
contents.abstract: Public opinion is a crucial driver of societal change and evolves through a complex interplay of individual belief change, generational turnover, and institutional influence. However, the dynamics of public opinion and its impact on the social structures that shape everyday life, vary from issue to issue. For example, while attitudes on gender roles and same-sex marriage have shifted steadily, reflected in both surveyed attitudes and policy change, other topics like abortion rights have oscillated or remained stagnant. To understand this heterogeneity, we introduce a dynamic model of long-term opinion dynamics that integrates two often overlooked forces: the replacement of older generations with younger ones, and endogenous feedback between public opinion and the policy environment. The model captures how individuals form beliefs based on inherited views, perceived behavioral norms, while also accounting for differences in lived experience and pushback against perceived extremes in policy. Policies and governing institutions are, in turn, shaped by individuals typically in an older demographic. Simulations reveal that this coupled opinion-policy system reproduces three characteristic trajectories in public opinion: steady change, long-term stagnation, and cyclical reversals. These dynamics are driven by issue-specific thresholds for belief change and the strength of resistance to policy. By explicitly modeling the endogeneity among public attitudes, norms, and policy, the framework explains why change for some social issues becomes self-reinforcing whereas others are prone to backlash. Our results highlight how institutional context and intergenerational dynamics jointly shape long-term public opinion and offer a simple, generalizable foundation for understanding when durable social change is likely to occur.

contents.title: Evaluating Beyond the Screen: Collective Assessment of AI-Generated Business Plans with Resource-Constrained Entrepreneurs
contents.abstract: Entrepreneurs increasingly use end-user generative AI technologies such as ChatGPT for high-stakes documents like loan applications and business plans, where AI-generated errors---a wrong price, a fabricated product---can affect loan or funding outcomes. Current approaches to supporting evaluation of AI-generated text assume a single user assessing output alone, on screen. This can be especially demanding for resource-constrained entrepreneurs, whose digital and AI skills vary widely. In this early-stage work, we explore how evaluation might instead be organized in a group setting and completed as a collective activity. We extended BizChat, an AI-powered business-planning tool, with an evaluation module that links each generated claim to the entrepreneur's original input. We partner with community organizations in Maryland---embedding BizChat within various entrepreneurship programs---where workshop attendees (N=14) evaluated their plans through think-pair-share discussion. Early findings suggest interface scaffolds like claim-to-input links primed attendees with concrete, personal evaluations, which the group setting then extended beyond the screen: attendees requested printed copies, used rubrics to compare across plans, and drew on peers' knowledge to verify what they could not easily judge alone.

contents.title: Evaluation and Best Practices of AI-Assisted Thematic Analysis
contents.abstract: Qualitative research underpins many insights and actions across a variety of contexts, and AI brings the possibility of performing this research in fractions of the time at similar or better quality. Testing frontier AI models’ ability to construct themes from public comments submitted to a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) policy document, we find that AI’s fit for this work is largely a function of its configuration. Our results show that output quality substantially increases with a thoughtfully engineered prompt and research question elaboration. We also find that different research questions and positionality profiles surface different theme sets while output quality holds. This understanding can inform new hybrid human-AI workflows in qualitative research.

contents.title: GeoVision: Designing a Complementary Human-AI Workflow for Cue-Based Geolocation
contents.abstract: Image geolocation, the process of determining the precise location on Earth where a photo or video was created, is a fundamental task for Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) analysts in many domains, including investigative journalism, law enforcement, and historical scholarship. We present GeoVision, a complementary human-AI workflow in which AI surfaces cues, retrieves guide knowledge, and ranks candidates, while humans reconcile conflicting evidence and make precise final judgments.

contents.title: Human vs AI Instruction in Multilingual Conversational Crowdsourcing: Effects on Crowdworker Performance, Efficiency and Interaction
contents.abstract: Language barriers remain a major challenge in multilingual crowdsourcing, where task instructions may differ from workers’ preferred languages. Recent advances in Large Language Model (LLM)s enable conversational Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems to provide context-aware guidance, but their use as multilingual instructional agents remains underexplored. This study examines how linguistically diverse crowdworkers communicate and perform under AI-mediated and human peer-mediated instruction. We developed a conversational annotation environment in which performers completed sequential bounding-box tasks while interacting with a human peer crowdworker instructor or a Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT)-4-based instructor through the same translation middleware. The analysis included 65 performers, with 34 assigned to the AI condition and 31 to the human peer-instruction condition. Annotation quality performance was evaluated using Intersection over Union (IoU), completion time, message volume, communication efficiency, and lexical interaction patterns. We found no evidence of a global difference in annotation quality between instructional conditions. Mixed-effects models also showed no systematic group differences across tasks or subtasks. Exploratory comparisons identified localized variation, but these findings were not confirmed by the corresponding interaction models. The performers under the AI-based training exchanged more messages, whereas peer instruction produced higher annotation quality per message. Lexical analysis indicated that AI instructor emphasized procedural actions, while the peer instructors used more annotation-oriented descriptions. Overall, conversational AI altered the structure of interaction without producing a detected reduction or a uniform improvement in annotation performance. These findings support the feasibility of automated and semi-automated instructional schemes for multilingual crowdsourcing, while highlighting that their value depends on task design and integration into the workflow

contents.title: Knowing When Humans Need More Help: Confidence-Aware Enterprise AI Decision Support
contents.abstract: Enterprise AI systems increasingly assist professionals in software engineering, operations, compliance, healthcare, and finance by providing recommendations that support complex decision making. Existing adaptive AI systems primarily estimate model confidence to determine response reliability, yet they rarely consider the confidence of the human decision maker. Consequently, AI assistance often remains static regardless of whether users are certain, hesitant, or overwhelmed. We propose Confidence-Aware Enterprise AI (CA-EAI), a human-centered framework that continuously estimates human decision confidence and dynamically adapts AI assistance accordingly. By incorporating behavioral, conversational, and contextual indicators of user confidence, the framework adjusts explanation depth, evidence presentation, and decision support without altering the underlying AI model. We present the conceptual architecture together with an illustrative proof-of-concept demonstrating how confidence-aware adaptation can improve decision quality, trust, and human-AI complementarity. This work positions human confidence as an essential signal for adaptive enterprise AI.

contents.title: Mental Models and Personalization of Model Selection
contents.abstract: According to the Rashomon set theory (Breiman, 2001), for any given task, multiple models — or the same model with different parameters — can achieve comparable performance (e.g., accuracy), even though their predictions may differ substantially across individual observations. Analogously, people may hold distinct mental models (e.g., different decision rules) for the same task while still attaining similar overall performance. This raises an important question: when a person collaborates with an AI model, does it matter whether that model aligns with their mental models? In this work, we investigate what happens when we minimize or maximize the discrepancy between a person’s mental model and the AI model they collaborate with, by matching participants with a model that is either similar to or different from their own mental model. Collaborating with a closely aligned model implies fewer points of disagreement — and thus fewer decisions about whether to adopt or override the AI’s recommendations — which saves time and cognitive effort, but also limits opportunities to improve or worsen. Conversely, collaborating with a model that differs markedly from their mental model leads to more frequent disagreement, making collaborative outcomes less predictable while providing richer opportunities for humans to update their understanding and potentially improve their decision-making. We address three research questions: (1) Do people prefer to collaborate with a model that aligns with their mental model? (2) Are people more likely to trust and adopt recommendations from an aligned model? (3) Are people better or worse off — in terms of decision quality — when supported by a model closely aligned with their mental model? We design two-stage experiments to investigate these questions. In the main study, Stage 1 participants make decisions independently, establishing a baseline of their individual decision-making patterns. We then select — from a pool of candidate models with comparable overall performance — a model most similar to, or most different from, each participant's mental model (as approximated by their observed decisions). In Stage 2, participants are randomly assigned to collaborate with either the most similar or the most different model, and we assess their adoption behavior and human-AI collaborative outcomes. In a separate study with a similar Stage 1 design, participants are shown both models in Stage 2 and asked to indicate their preference. The study is currently in the data collection phase.

contents.title: Multi-Agent Debate for Human-AI Decision-Making
contents.abstract: We explore leveraging multi-agent debate (MAD) for human-AI decision-making. Through a user study on a LLM-response error-detection task, we find that MAD can outperform single-AI assistance and single-round interaction when users actively participate in the debate, while forcing diversity in AIs' answers could hurt task performance.

contents.title: Performance, Suggestion Adoption, and Trust in Iterative AI-Assisted Ideation
contents.abstract: AI-assisted ideation is increasingly used to support creative design tasks, yet little is known about how repeated interaction shapes performance, suggestion adoption, and trust over time. This study examines AI-assisted ideation as an iterative human-AI interaction process. This study examines AI-assisted ideation as an iterative human-AI interaction process using data from the AI Design Assistant (AIDA) framework. Mixed-effects models were used to analyze turn-level and session-level data from 219 creative ideation sessions involving 73 users. The result indicated that creative performance improvements did not stem from sudden breakthroughs triggered by specific AI responses but followed a trajectory of incremental accumulation across interaction turns. The extent of adoption of AI suggestions could not reliably predict sustained performance gains, suggesting a disconnect between behavioral adoption and objective outcomes. Conversely, trust was more strongly associated with affective characteristics of AI responses and was further shaped by user input features. These findings suggest that performance, adoption, and trust should be understood as related but distinct processes in AI-assisted ideation. The study highlights the value of a process-oriented and longitudinal perspective for understanding human-AI collaboration in creative design tasks.

contents.title: PersonaSmith: Human-Centered Calibration of LLM Personas through Dynamic Profile Optimization
contents.abstract: LLM personas are increasingly used to shape the tone, style, and social behavior of conversational AI, yet persona authoring remains largely ad hoc: designers write static trait descriptions, inspect a few outputs, and manually revise prompts until the agent "feels right". We frame LLM persona design as a human-centered calibration problem: a useful persona should express an intended trait consistently, stay interpretable to its designer, transfer across models where possible, and let the designer choose an appropriate intensity. We present PersonaSmith, a black-box optimization framework that iteratively refines structured persona profiles from situational personality feedback. Rather than optimizing free-form prompts, it preserves human-readable profile fields—career, values, hobbies, and behavioral tendencies—so the resulting personas remain inspectable and reusable. On TRAIT and MPI, optimized profiles elicit stronger Big-Five expression than prior persona prompts, with the largest gains on mid-sized models. The optimization trajectory further exposes intermediate points that designers can use to set personality intensity. A human evaluation confirms that people perceive PersonaSmith personas as more trait-consistent than, and comparably natural to, baseline prompts. Together, these results suggest that LLM persona design should be treated not as one-shot prompt writing, but as iterative, measurable, and human-verifiable calibration.

contents.title: Right Advice, Wrong Reasons: Effect of Reasoning Alignment on Trust and Reliance in AI Advisors
contents.abstract: People increasingly turn to AI systems for everyday decisions, forming a new kind of advisory relationship. Many of these decisions are personal and moral, such as whether to report a colleague or whether to tell a friend something they would rather not hear. Such advice now constitutes a substantial share of what people ask LLMs for. As agentic systems mature, people are no longer only consulting AI but also delegating decisions to it—letting it draft messages, screen candidates, and act on their behalf. Advice-taking requires only momentary agreement, whereas delegation requires trust. What earns that trust remains unclear. When asked directly, people rate AI advisors as less trustworthy than human advisors, even though AI-generated moral advice is rated as more thoughtful and correct than advice from a human expert and can shift human judgments. Recent work suggests that these findings are not necessarily in tension. AI advice can shift judgments even when no justification accompanies it, and deference appears to track the verdict more than the reasoning behind it. In other words, an AI advisor can sway judgments without being trusted. But if the recommendation carries persuasion, this leaves open what the reasoning carries. Existing findings do not reveal which component of the advice earns which form of reliance. Three gaps remain. First, judgments and reasoning have not been varied independently: an advisor’s justification typically supports the recommendation it accompanies. Second, when reasoning has been varied, studies have manipulated its quality or presence, rather than whether it appeals to the values a person holds. This distinction matters because, especially in high-stakes settings, people may care not only about what a system decides but also whether its decision process is one they recognize and endorse. Third, persuasion has been the primary outcome of interest, leaving open whether judgment alignment and reasoning alignment shape trust and reliance differently, as prior findings suggest they might. Closing these gaps requires connecting disciplines. We draw on value theory from moral psychology to recover, for each individual, both the decision they would favor and the reasons they would find important. We then use this profile to control an LLM advisor’s advice, bringing a measurement framework from psychology to a question in human–AI interaction. In this ongoing work, we investigate how alignment between AI moral advice and a user’s preferred judgment, compared with alignment between the AI’s reasoning and the user’s values, influences user trust, willingness to rely on the advice, and willingness to delegate tasks to the AI. We built a study framework that varies AI judgment and value-related reasoning independently within a moral dilemma task. Participants will complete a values questionnaire, and we will project their scores onto the value axis underlying each dilemma to recover, for each individual, both the judgment they would favor and the value considerations they would find important. An LLM advisor will then deliver advice that independently matches or mismatches each of these dimensions, so alignment is defined relative to the individual rather than to a fixed stance.

contents.title: Should an Expert Specialize, Synthesize, or Speculate? Discovering Latent Clusters and Ensemble Probabilities through Bandit-Arm Bid Search and Arbitrage
contents.abstract: Expertise formation is an emergent process, given how experts imitate discovery patterns and synthesize knowledge across domains. This paper draws from collective intelligence research, hierarchy-of-hypotheses synthesis approaches, and agent-based modeling to explore how scientific communities stabilize, fragment, expire, and regenerate around exploratory reward structures. Knowledge “stock” and incommensurability fluctuate as competing epistemic currencies are reconfigured as sets across domains (programmed as bandit arm networks). Epistemic payoffs are modeled as density dependent, in which the effective explanatory utility of a paradigm decreases as excessive consensus forms around it, while conversely the relative value of payoff may increase, so that new ideas become expensive. This either disincentivizes occupying “conventional” ideas, or can encourage a speculative rush. Secondly, agents are rewarded for discovering a structural hypothesis coupling between arms, but there’s a cost to infer and test equivalence categorically. This simulates the danger drawing extensive theories across disciplines. Bandit arms are compared as binomial sequences with pattern sets tested using Jaccardian similarity. Where strong signal matches are found, that defy a lag across a network, then agents accrue compounded rewards through an ensemble of probabilities—with a diversified epistemic currency portfolio. Agents can pursue a two-fold incentive reward scheme: navigating and accruing a distant set of payouts, while facing penalties for broadness, or committing themselves to a single rewarding bandit, which may face low demand, but perhaps will be prone to attracting overcrowding by experts from other fields.

contents.title: Temporal Alignment Impacts Human–AI collaboration in a Cooperative Task
contents.abstract: Human-AI teams often fail to achieve complementarity, even when AI systems outperform humans in isolation. Recent theories of Human-AI teaming and collective human-machine intelligence suggest that effective collaboration depends not only on complementary capabilities but also on coordination mechanisms that enable humans and AI to function as teammates. One such mechanism may be temporal alignment: the synchronization of actions, adaptation, and decision timing between human and AI teammates. Despite its importance in teamwork research, temporal alignment has rarely been studied directly in Human-AI collaboration. We investigate the role of temporal alignment in a fast-paced cooperative task using the Overcooked environment. Across two studies, we compare Human-only, AI-only, and Human-AI teams. In Study 1, participants were paired with a self-play reinforcement learning agent operating at its native speed, creating temporal misalignment between human and AI teammates. Human-AI teams failed to achieve complementarity and exhibited highly imbalanced contributions. In Study 2, the same AI policy was constrained to operate at human-like speeds, isolating temporal alignment from AI capability. Temporal alignment substantially improved collaboration: complementarity increased, workload became more balanced, and distinct patterns of role specialization emerged, with humans and AI contributing to different task functions. Participants also reported greater enjoyment and perceived the temporally aligned AI as more human-like. These findings demonstrate that temporal alignment is a key factor towards the emergence of Human-AI complementarity. Thus, we propose that effective Human-AI teams depend not only on the intelligence of agents, but also on the ability for AI teammates to coordinate in time with humans.

contents.title: Where AI Helps a Design Workflow—and Where It Does Not: Stage-Level Human–AI Complementarity in Multi-Agent Design Thinking
contents.abstract: Where AI contributes to a multi-stage creative workflow such as Design Thinking (DT)—and where human judgment must lead—remains unclear. We present AX·DT, a multi-agent system spanning the five DT stages: role-specialized agents draft artifacts, an orchestration layer forwards user-approved versions across stages, and users author every final artifact. In an exploratory controlled comparison (n=12) with an analog workflow, AX·DT shortened the first four stages by 46.2% and raised expert-rated artifact quality—but unevenly: gains concentrated on structured prototype artifacts, shrank for idea creativity, and reversed for interpreting users' emotional states, a preliminary sketch of stage-level human–AI complementarity in creative workflows.

contents.title: Which Piece Should I Play Next? Human--AI Collaboration for Personalized Music-Difficulty Assessment
contents.abstract: Music platforms have typically focused on recommending songs for listeners. In this work, we expand the recommendation capabilities to assist amateur musicians in selecting scores they can realistically perform. Existing methods often rely on difficulty labels that are sparse, inconsistent, and typically apply globally rather than being tailored to individual performers. To address this issue, we propose a human-AI collaboration framework where AI analyzes symbolic scores at scale, while musicians maintain control over their goals, ability profiles, and final repertoire choices. The system learns from human assessments of difficulty, identifies challenging passages by analyzing overlapping sections of scores, and personalizes recommendations based on a musician's skills and objectives. Additionally, structured score evidence helps to provide clear explanations in natural language. The division of labor is well-defined: AI offers scalable screening and localization, whereas musicians contribute context, make corrections, oversee the process, and hold final authority over decisions. We outline the system architecture and propose an evaluation plan that focuses on recommendation quality, calibration, adaptation, and appropriate reliance on AI.

contents.title: 2027 announcements
American Memory: A brief history of efforts to make Library of Congress materials broadly available since the beginning of the web
contents.abstract: The Library of Congress has been leading and participating in efforts to make digital collections available online for more than 30 years. In 1995, Entertainment Weekly Magazine listed the Library of Congress site "American Memory" as one of the "Five Best Websites." Since then, Library of Congress staff have relied on a range of techniques and technologies to engage the American people with the information held on their behalf in the oldest federal cultural heritage institution in the United States (and the largest library in the world). Successive and overlapping strategies of curated websites, institutional collaboration, mass digitization, single-search-interfaces, crowdsourcing, collections-as-data, and machine learning through to contemporary uses of AI have challenged us to think across the disparate scales of human knowledge, cultural memory, and individual learning. As a way to explore these issues, the talk will describe a recent program from the Library of Congress to operate at the scale of local communities by co-creating digital experiences onsite inside public libraries, institutions whose approach to tackling the problems of scale offers an interesting complement to the challenges we face at the national level.

contents.title: After MTurk
contents.abstract: Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk), a platform that has shaped human computation and crowdsourcing research for nearly two decades, is set to sunset on September 30, 2026—the final day of HCOMP 2026. This panel brings together researchers with extensive experience studying and using MTurk to reflect on the platform’s impact, discuss what its closure means for researchers and workers, and consider what comes next. Looking beyond MTurk, the panel will explore the future of online crowd work, research platforms, and human participation in an era increasingly shaped by AI.

contents.title: Anchored Minds, Collective Foresight: How Collective Intelligence Reshapes the Perceived Ruggedness of a Smooth Problem
contents.abstract: How do independent solvers, none of whom succeeds alone, navigate a hard problem — and does coordination help or hurt? We study 96 people who, without communication, reverse-engineered the same hidden causal structure (a 3- or 4-node Bayesian network), with every belief revision logged at one-second resolution. Individually, human search is an anchored, truncated-Lévy walk — bold excursions whose progress peaks at an intermediate jump size, plus productive returns to good solutions — yet it is confined and ultra-slow: no participant ever reached the solution. Strikingly, although the solution space is objectively smooth (a single basin), people behave as if it were rugged. We reconstruct this perceived landscape from the trajectories, showing that ruggedness lives in the solver, not the problem — and that the collective mode reshapes it. Independent aggregation exposes shared false peaks: non-solution attractors that many independent participants settle on and that replicate across disjoint halves of the crowd (meanwhile the crowd's best-of-N improves as a power law, D_min ~ N^(−b), b ≈ 0.4, with near-linear coverage). Costly knowledge exchange then collapses the rugged effective landscape into a single consensus basin — solving the problem no individual solved, but at the cost of coverage, and risking premature convergence when exchange is too cheap. A simulation calibrated to the measured search dynamics reproduces all three regimes. The effective ruggedness is thus not a property of the problem but of how the collective is organized: independent aggregation preserves the diverse exploration that charts the space, whereas costly communication trades that diversity for rapid consensus — clarifying when each mode best serves collective problem-solving.

contents.title: Hackalysis: Detecting Hackathon-Origin Software Through Temporal and Structural Repository Traces
contents.abstract: Hackathons are among the most visible contemporary sites of time-bounded collective innovation: self-organizing teams converge for one to three days to build working software prototypes. Once an event ends, however, the repositories these teams leave behind are difficult to identify within the broader open-source ecosystem. Because hackathon repositories are rapid prototypes rather than sustained projects, conflating them with long-lived software distorts analyses of repository health, maintenance, and open-source sustainability. This paper presents Hackalysis, a metadata-driven framework for detecting and characterizing hackathon-origin GitHub repositories using only publicly available signals. From LauzHack (2023–2025) and an expert-curated control set of sustained academic and professional open-source projects, a labeled dataset of 458 repositories with complete GitHub metadata is constructed. Temporal, activity, social, and structural features are derived, and four classification strategies of increasing complexity are compared: rule-based scoring, correlation-weighted scoring, a Random Forest classifier, and an unweighted majority-voting consensus. A modest Random Forest is the strongest of the four (87.1% accuracy, 0.946 AUC-ROC under 5-fold cross-validation), and the majority-voting consensus does not improve on it. Across all methods, hackathon-origin repositories exhibit a consistent dual signature: concentrated development bursts together with structural minimalism, including markedly lower prevalence of tests, CI/CD workflows, deployment configuration, documentation, licenses, and contribution guidelines. The single most discriminative signal is the active-development window: hackathon repositories concentrate essentially all commits within a 1–3 day burst. These results show that short-term collective innovation leaves detectable behavioral and structural traces in software repositories, and provide a reproducible basis for isolating innovation-contest software and studying how its outputs relate to the sustained open-source ecosystem around them.

contents.title: Worse Leader Quality Resulted in More Coordinated But Less Adaptive Voting Patterns in a Dynamic Environment
contents.abstract: Governance structures capture how groups make collective decisions among options. Existing research has examined both how groups choose governance structures, such as Majority Voting or Leader Decisions, and how these structures affect group performance. The present work bridges these two research streams with an experiment in which groups of four participants repeatedly vote between options with dynamic values. First, we examine how the dynamic performance of groups using Majority Voting and Leader Decisions affected when groups switched between them. Second, we examine how the dynamic performance of a group using either Majority Voting or Leader Decisions influenced their voting behaviour within that structure. Our contribution is to examine whether reinforcement learning of both governance structure and option value can account for participants’ voting behaviour in a dynamic environment. We manipulated the Leader quality between groups. Bad Leader groups swapped more consistently to Majority Voting. Surprisingly, we found that groups with Bad Leaders coordinated their option voting better than groups with Good Leaders. However, computational modelling captured how the more deterministic voting of Bad Leader groups caused a “status quo bias” that led to Bad Leader groups adapting worse to change and scoring worse than Good Leader groups.

contents.title: Identifying Broadly Effective Approaches for Users with Different Abilities
contents.abstract: Crowdsourcing and open competitions are often used to evaluate and select approaches or methods for solving complex tasks. In such competitions, participants with heterogeneous abilities try candidate approaches or methods, and the platform selects a method based on realized scores. Among such methods, a useful method achieves robust performance across users with heterogeneous abilities, rather than performing well only when used by experts. A natural way to select such a method is to ask participants to try candidate methods and compare their realized scores. However, the realized scores may reflect not only the intrinsic performance of each method but also participants’ abilities and effort induced by rewards. We study how a platform can select a method that performs well across users with heterogeneous abilities. The platform assigns methods to participants, offers score-based rewards under a finite budget, and selects a method from the realized scores. We analyze two selection procedures under different assumptions about how ability and effort are related to scores. First, when this relationship is unknown, we consider a selection procedure that assigns a single method per participant and pays linear rewards. Second, when the relationship follows a power-law form with an unknown exponent, we consider a selection procedure that assigns all methods to all participants. We also provide a guarantee on selection correctness for each procedure. Experiments support the theoretical findings and show when each procedure is effective.

contents.title: Social learning drives underprioritization of collective challenges
contents.abstract: Societies often struggle to prioritize competing challenges in a timely manner, with substantial costs from delayed action on issues like climate change and pandemic mitigation. A persistent puzzle is that broad concern often fails to translate into collective priority, as with climate relative to the economy. Most models of opinion dynamics analyze issues in isolation and cannot explain how competing concerns with inherent trade-offs are reconciled into collective priority. We argue that a key driver is the differing reliance on social learning across domains. Some issues rely heavily on social learning, inferring importance from others, because direct experience is limited; others rely more on individual learning from firsthand experience, as with economic conditions. To identify endogenous mechanisms driving this mis-prioritization, we develop a dynamic model in which individuals in two subgroups form issue-specific concerns through social and individual learning, aggregated into collective priority. The model yields three insights. First, at equal objective severity, issues that depend more on social learning are systematically mis-prioritized. Second, when social learning is high, gradual increases in severity may not raise collective priority, producing delayed action or persistent misalignment. Third, cross-group learning can mitigate this bias, but only above a critical threshold. Two levers can realign collective priority with severity. One is sustained cross-group engagement that pushes inter-group learning past the threshold. The other is strengthening firsthand experience of an issue, reducing reliance on social cues.

blocks.name: Evaluation, Annotation, and Oversight of AI

contents.title: FIBB: Capturing False Information Beliefs and Behaviors Across Physical and Online Environments
contents.abstract: Humans assess the veracity of newly presented false information using multiple sources: from observations in the online environment (e.g., social media content or responses from AI-mediated systems) to observations in the physical world (e.g., current state of the world or other people's behaviors). Belief in false information can lead to adverse societal and physical consequences, including impacts on health and emergency response decisions, increased strain on public resources, and decreased public trust. Currently, false information datasets are limited to examining either online or physical behaviors, making it difficult to evaluate the impact of false claims holistically across environments. Moreover, retrieving beliefs and behaviors across topics at scale through traditional methods, such as user surveys, can be time- and resource-intensive. To address these gaps, we propose a False Information Dataset Containing Beliefs and Behaviors Across Physical and Online Environments (FIBB). FIBB comprises 1,500 LLM-generated scenarios grounded on 300 online false claims in natural disasters (e.g., hurricanes, wildfires, earthquakes) and health (e.g., COVID-19, mental health, chronic diseases). Leveraging cognitive science principles, each FIBB scenario cycles through a person's veracity assessment and decision-making by depicting their mental states, observations, actions, and the changes in the world resulting from their actions. By bridging the gap between online and physical environments, FIBB aims to inform future downstream goals, such as facilitating the development of world models that can represent people's likely beliefs and behavioral consequences of false information in tandem.

contents.title: Information Satisfaction: A Reader-Centered Axis for Summarization Evaluation
contents.abstract: The majority of work on summarization evaluation focuses on general summary quality (e.g., ROUGE, BERTScore) or specific desired properties (e.g., readability, factuality). However, these metrics fail to measure the utility of a summary to an individual user. For example, a biomedical researcher learning about the latest vaccine research will have different informational needs than a family doctor. Query-focused summarization captures part of this need, but in practice users rarely state everything relevant in a query, so the same short query underspecifies what a researcher versus a physician actually wants. A reader's persona, meaning their role and expertise, is comparatively stable across queries and recovers much of this missing context, which makes it a practical signal for evaluating whether a summary satisfies the reader. We therefore test how sensitive popular summarization metrics are to both informational and persona differences, and find that many popular metrics, including strong LLM-as-judge metrics, fail basic perturbation tests of informational content. We additionally conduct an expert human evaluation, in which we measure summary preferences based on information satisfaction in relation to a specific person's background and use case. We find that both traditional and LLM-based metrics are insufficient measures of information satisfaction and agree poorly with human judgment.

contents.title: Enhancing LLM-Based Data Annotation through Error Decomposition: A Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation Paradigm
contents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative to human coding for data annotation tasks, enabling the scale-up of research across data-intensive domains such as learning analytics. While LLMs are already achieving near-human accuracy on objective annotation tasks, their performance on subjective annotation tasks, such as those involving psychological constructs, is less consistent and more prone to errors. Standard evaluation practices typically collapse all annotation errors into a single alignment metric, but this simplified approach may obscure different kinds of errors that affect final analytical conclusions in different ways. Here, we propose a diagnostic evaluation paradigm that incorporates a human-in-the-loop step to separate task-inherent ambiguity from model-driven inaccuracies and assess annotation quality in terms of their potential downstream impacts. We refine this paradigm on ordinal annotation tasks, which are common in subjective annotation. The refined paradigm includes: (1) a diagnostic taxonomy that categorizes LLM annotation errors along two dimensions: source (model-specific vs. task-inherent) and type (boundary ambiguity vs. conceptual misidentification); (2) a lightweight human annotation test to estimate task-inherent ambiguity from LLM annotations; and (3) a computational method to decompose observed LLM annotation errors following our taxonomy. We validate this paradigm on four educational annotation tasks, demonstrating both its conceptual validity and practical utility. Theoretically, our work provides empirical evidence for why excessively high alignment is unrealistic in specific annotation tasks and why single alignment metrics inadequately reflect the quality of LLM annotations. In practice, our paradigm can be a low-cost diagnostic tool that assesses the suitability of a given task for LLM annotation and provides actionable insights for further technical optimization.

contents.title: Beyond Truth Discovery: A Two-Stage Framework to Assess the Severity of False Claim during Disasters
contents.abstract: False information spreads rapidly on social media during disasters and can undermine emergency response efforts, public trust, and crisis communication. Existing research primarily focuses on determining whether social media posts contain false information, but provides limited insight into the specific false claims embedded within posts and the severity of individual false claims. To address the limitations, we propose a two-stage framework to assess the severity of false claims during disasters. In the first stage, we develop fasle claim extraction agent that identifies false claims from multimodal social media posts containing text, images, videos, and external links. A subsequent verification step validates extracted claims against supporting evidence. In the second stage, we define false claim severity as the combination of two complementary dimensions: believability, which captures the likelihood that a claim will be believed, and harmfulness, which captures the potential consequences if it is believed. Human annotators assess both dimensions to construct a claim-level severity benchmark. Building upon this benchmark, we investigate false claim severity assessment as a human-AI alignment problem. Rather than directly predicting severity labels, we evaluate whether models can reproduce the judgments made by human annotators under a shared evaluation rubric. Experiments on Reddit posts collected during hurricanes and wildfires show that traditional supervised models exhibit limited alignment with human severity judgments, whereas LLMs achieve substantially stronger performance. Among the evaluated strategies, in-context learning consistently achieves the strongest alignment with human judgments, highlighting the importance of human examples and shared decision criteria for severity assessment.

contents.title: From Answers to Audit Opinions: Cost-Aware Expert Verification of Financial Artifacts from Tool-Using LLM Agents
contents.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly produce financial artifacts such as ratio tables, evidence-backed memos, and spreadsheet-style analyses. Existing evaluations often reduce such outputs to binary correctness or faithfulness labels, overlooking whether the artifact has sufficient evidence, whether errors are material or pervasive, and whether evidence gaps should prevent acceptance. We adapt audit-opinion logic to agentic artifact verification as a research-label framework with four labels: Clean, Qualified, Adverse, and Disclaimer. The proposed audit certificate turns each artifact into a checkable workpaper by linking claims to provenance, formulas, verification outcomes, scope limits, and Critical Artifact Matters. Our evaluation package combines SEC-backed cases, oracle-backed injected failures, expert adjudication, blind re-audit, hard-case stress diagnostics, and an expanded 400-case oracle-backed checker-field diagnostic. In the expanded diagnostic, full-certificate checker fields remove false-clean labels that remain common under artifact-only and partial-certificate views. The completed Phase 3 expert batch shows that oracle-backed perturbation labels and expert audit opinions diverge in materiality-sensitive cases, while blind re-audit shows substantial within-expert stability.

contents.title: SleuthTalk: Supporting Historical Photo Identification with Private Workspaces for Collective Sensemaking and Deliberation
contents.abstract: Identifying individuals in historical photographs is a critical task across fields such as history, journalism, genealogy, and archival research. While AI-based facial recognition can efficiently generate candidate matches, it often produces ambiguous results that require deeper analysis and contextual interpretation. Existing platforms lack robust support for collaborative deliberation, especially in uncertain or high-stakes cases. We present SleuthTalk, a private collaborative workspace integrated into Civil War Photo Sleuth, designed to scaffold structured comparison, discussion, and group decision-making. SleuthTalk enables users to curate custom shortlists, annotate facial features, and build consensus through structured feedback. In a mixed-methods evaluation with experienced historical photo researchers, SleuthTalk enhanced confidence, surfaced diverse perspectives, and supported more transparent, reflective identifications.

contents.title: Disentangling Threads: Exploring the Potential of LLM-Supported Discussion Forum Analysis for Community Insight
contents.abstract: Online discussion forums enable people from diverse backgrounds to share ideas, feedback, and perspectives. These organic discussions can help researchers understand communities’ collective viewpoints, but insights are often difficult to uncover given their freeform reply structure. Large language models (LLMs) support qualitative text analysis but can misalign with researchers' analytical intent and miss key insights. To inform design considerations for forum sensemaking tools, we manually analyzed a forum discussion, synthesized an analysis framework from relevant literature, built a research probe, and interviewed 21 researchers to explore perceived opportunities and barriers with LLM representations of collective discussions. We provide recommendations for community sensemaking tools to support flexible analytical goals grounded in raw user data and enable follow-up research processes, while balancing commenter identity with open expression in forums.

contents.title: Metacognitive AI and Peer Information in Collective Decisions
contents.abstract: Groups are assembled to improve decision quality, yet collective judgments often inherit and amplify individual biases. Group performance depends on how influence is allocated across members, and confidence that is misaligned with expertise degrades that allocation and the resulting decision. As organizations increasingly embed generative AI into decision processes, we ask whether an AI that elicits reasoning, without suggesting answers, can improve the inputs to group deliberation. We study \emph{metacognitive assistance}: a Socratic-style agent that asks principals to articulate assumptions and consider counterevidence before they deliberate. We have built an online experimental platform and run two single-participant pilots. Socratic elicitation recalibrates confidence, withdrawing it from initially-incorrect answers and reinforcing it in initially-correct ones, consistent with our hypothesis; whether this reallocates influence within real groups remains open for the full experiment.

contents.title: Conversational Forecasting using Hyperchat AI vs a large-scale Prediction Market
contents.abstract: This proposed talk will cover a new method for harnessing the collective intelligence of networked human groups referred to as "Conversational Forecasting." As the name implies, this new method enables a networked human teams of potentially any size (from a handful of participants to hundreds ) to discuss and debate a forecastable event and have that conversation automatically converge on a rigorous prediction that accurately reflects the collective insight of the group. In addition, because this method uses natural conversation, the output is not merely a probabilistic forecast but a rigorous assessment of the reasoning behind the forecast (i.e. the most influential arguments in favor and the most influential counterpoints). This conversational CI method leverages an agentic framework of intervening AI agents referred to as Hyperchat AI. In addition, this talk will review the results of a pilot study that tasked 25 sports fans with conversationally forecasting 50 NBA basketball games against the spread. Results show that when discussing and debating NBA games (for 5 minutes each) using a collaboration platform called Thinkscape, human teams were 62% accurate across a set of 50 forecasted NBA games. This was a very promising result when compared to the Vegas odds of 50% (p=0.059). Furthermore, had the participants wagered on the games, they would have produced an 18.4% ROI over the 12-week period. In addition, this study found that the group’s conversation rate during each forecast was positively correlated with their prediction accuracy. In fact, when excluding the 12 forecasts in the bottom 25th percentile by average conversation rate, the remaining 38 forecasts recorded a 68% accuracy, significantly better than the 50% Vegas odds (p=0.017). This result also outperformed the well-known prediction market Polymarket (p=0.062) which was 54.6% accurate across the same set of NBA games. Overall, these outcomes suggest that real-time large-scale conversational deliberations, when facilitated by AI agents, can amplify collective intelligence during human forecasting tasks while also surfacing the most influential arguments and counterpoints that drove the forecast to converge the way it did.

contents.title: Preference-based deliberation optimizes for endorsement, not efficiency
contents.abstract: AI mediators such as the Habermas Machine aggregate many individual opinions into a single group statement that participants endorse. I ask whether such endorsement also tracks the efficiency of the resulting decision. To examine this, I build a coupled common-pool resource model and deliberate over it with a simplified Habermas Machine that ranks synthesized statements and selects among them by the Schulze method. Because the efficient allocation is placed on every ballot, a failure to elect it reflects what participants endorse rather than a failure to generate it. Two failure modes arise even when the group jointly holds enough information to identify the optimum. Participants who hold only a partial view of the system rank the optimum below their own ideal and out-vote it, and when participants disagree on the efficient policy, no value commands a majority and pools are left uncommitted. As a consequence, a uniformly uninformed electorate can outperform a divided one, and increasing the number of coupled pools buries the optimum further for participants who misread the system's structure.
